P2B00.d: P2B00 says the engine module could not confirm, with the engine past its cold-start phase, that injection pulses it commanded for cylinder 1 really happened. GM documents the check for its petrol direct-injection engines: the ECM digitises the voltage across both injector wires and looks for the small flux signature the armature leaves when it lifts.
s: Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 1 (P0301), sometimes no noticeable symptom
With a harness short, several unrelated codes at once and possibly a no-start
c: Engine harness chafed through to ground (GM L3B – above the camshaft carrier or near the left shock tower)
Armature or needle of the cylinder 1 injector sticking, so no opening signature appears
Outdated ECM calibration (GM service update for the 1.2 L LIH)
High contact resistance at the cylinder 1 injector connector

P2B01.d: P2B01 is stored when the ECM keeps missing the opening signature of the cylinder 2 injector in normal running, i.e. it has no proof that fuel was delivered on that cylinder's commanded pulses.
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Uneven idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 2
Together with many other codes and erratic behaviour when the harness is shorted
c: Engine harness shorted to ground at a chafe point (GM L3B bulletin series PIT5677)
Cylinder 2 injector opening sluggishly or not at all (deposits, worn armature)
Corroded or loose injector 2 connector distorting the feedback voltage

P2B02.d: P2B02 concerns cylinder 3: in warm operation the ECM did not see the voltage bump that marks the cylinder 3 injector actually opening, often enough to count pulses as not delivered. On GM's 1.2 L LIH three-cylinder, cylinder 3 is the last one, and the 2025 table for that family (cylinders 1–3 only) decides after 50 to 100 samples, Type B.
s: Check engine light, often without any driveability complaint
On a real injector fault rough running on cylinder 3 (P0303)
c: ECM calibration with false detections (GM 1.2 L LIH, service update A202310450)

P2B03.d: With P2B03 the engine module reports that cylinder 4 injection pulses went unconfirmed after warm-up: the coil voltage showed no proof of the armature moving. In GM's lists the code belongs to four-cylinder direct-injection engines – the three-cylinder tables end at P2B02 – and GM's 2025 four-cylinder table needs 50 to 100 samples for a Type B verdict with two trips.
s: Lamp on after the second faulty trip
Possibly misfire on cylinder 4 (P0304) or under load
Further injector codes of the same cylinder stored at the same time
c: Harness chafed near the turbo actuator or elsewhere on the engine (GM 2.7 L)
Poor contact in the fuel rail injector connector

P2B04.d: P2B04 extends the warm-running missed-pulse check to cylinder 5, so it only matters on engines with five or more cylinders. No manufacturer documents P2B04 publicly as a monitor of its own.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 5 (P0305)
c: Cylinder 5 injector sticking or opening too slowly
Chafed or high-resistance wiring to injector 5
Calibration error in the engine software

P2B05.d: P2B05 marks missed injection pulses on cylinder 6 outside the cold-start window; on a six-cylinder engine this is the last cylinder in the order of numbers. No manufacturer documents P2B05 publicly as a stand-alone check.
s: Check engine light
Slight shaking at idle or low speed, misfire on cylinder 6 (P0306)
c: Deposits or wear on the cylinder 6 injector hampering small pulses
Contact problem at the injector 6 plug
Injector driver or voltage sensing in the ECM faulty

P2B06.d: P2B06 is the warm-engine pulse check for cylinder 7 and so practically limited to V8 and larger engines. No manufacturer documents P2B06 publicly in its own entry.
s: Engine light on after two trips
Misfire on cylinder 7 (P0307), rough idle
c: Cylinder 7 injector with weak or missing armature lift
Wiring to injector 7 damaged by heat or chafing
Rail pressure outside the plausible range, distorting the opening signal

P2B07.d: P2B07 closes the warm-running row at cylinder 8, and the engine-wide check counting missed pulses over all cylinders is P2B96. No manufacturer documents P2B07 publicly as a separate monitor; GM's 2025 V8 tables mention it only in the code lists of shared calibration tables, while their cylinder 8 warm faults run as P10B1/P10B2.
s: Check engine light
Misfire on cylinder 8 (P0308), especially at idle
c: Heat-damaged harness section at the rear of the engine

P2B08.d: P2B08 is the cold-start version of the cylinder 1 pulse check. While the catalyst is being heated, many direct-injection engines split each injection into two or three small pulses, and CARB requires for 20/50/100 % of model years 2026/2027/2028 that missing split or multiple pulses be detected during the cold-start strategy.
s: Warning lamp, often with the engine running normally once warm
Possibly slightly rough running in the first seconds after a cold start
Code returns only after a long standstill, not on warm restarts
c: Cold-start software anomaly (GM 1.2 L LIH, fixed by ECM reprogramming)
Cylinder 1 injector sluggish when cold, missing the short split pulses
Contact fault in injector 1 wiring that shows mainly when cold

P2B09.d: P2B09 reports that while the catalyst is being warmed after a cold start the ECM missed the opening trace of injector 2 on too many commanded pulses. CARB defines the window: at least six hours engine-off, ambient at or above −6.7 °C and coolant no more than 15 °C warmer than ambient.
s: Check engine light after cold starts on two trips
Usually no driveability issue once the engine is warm
c: Cylinder 2 injector not responding to the short cold-start pulses
Wiring or connector problem on injector 2

P2B0A.d: P2B0A stands for missed cold-start pulses on cylinder 3. For the GM 1.2 L LIH with its three cylinders it is the highest cold-start cylinder code, since that engine's 2025 table stops at P2B0A.
s: Lamp on, code stored only after a cold start
Engine runs normally once warm
c: ECM software anomaly on the GM 1.2 L LIH (service update A202310450)
Cylinder 3 injector reacting too slowly when cold

P2B0B.d: P2B0B covers cylinder 4 during the cold-start strategy and in GM's tables belongs to four-cylinder and larger engines. GM's 2025 four-cylinder table sets the window via P2B95 differently from the three-cylinder: catalyst below 400 °C, 450–2,800 rpm, pedal up to 35 % and less than 100 s run time, so the test may continue while pulling away.
s: Warning lamp after cold starts
Possibly slightly uneven running during the first minute
c: ECM calibration needing an update (GM bulletin 20-NA-230)
Harness damage or poor contact at the fuel rail connector (GM 2.7 L)
Cylinder 4 injector sluggish at low temperature

P2B0C.d: P2B0C flags cylinder 5 when its injector fails to show an opening signature on the split pulses used to heat the catalyst after a cold start. Publicly it is documented only by GM, in the 2025 V8 table 25OBDG06A, which lists the cold-start codes for all eight cylinders (P2B08–P2B0F): Type B, decision after 50 to 100 samples.
s: Check engine light after two cold-start trips
Usually unremarkable running once warm, maybe a short rough idle when cold
c: Cylinder 5 injector not lifting on the short cold-start pulses
Injector 5 wiring or connector with a contact fault
ECM calibration issue (check for software updates)

P2B0D.d: P2B0D belongs to the cold-start family and points at cylinder 6: while the engine was splitting injections to heat the catalyst, the ECM failed to register the armature-lift voltage signature on too many of that injector's pulses. GM publishes it in the 2025 V8 table 25OBDG06A as Type B with a verdict after 50 to 100 samples.
s: Check engine light after two cold starts with the fault
Uneven idle in the first minute after a cold start, later normal
c: Cylinder 6 injector opening sluggishly on short pulses when cold (deposits, worn armature)
Corroded connector or chafed wire at injector 6 distorting the feedback voltage
ECM calibration detecting the opening signature unreliably in the cold-start phase

P2B0E.d: P2B0E is the cylinder 7 entry of the cold-start pulse check. On engines that fire two or three short injections per cycle while heating the catalyst, the ECM expects each of them to show an opening signature on the injector feedback voltage; for cylinder 7 too many did not.
s: Warning lamp after the second faulty cold start
Slight shaking right after a cold start, often nothing noticeable
c: Cylinder 7 injector not lifting on the very short split pulses (deposits, armature wear)
Enable or command wire of injector 7 damaged, falsifying the measured voltage
ECM software with an overly strict opening-signature evaluation

P2B0F.d: P2B0F closes the cold-start series with cylinder 8, so it only appears on eight-cylinder engines; publicly GM documents it, in table 25OBDG06A for its 2025 V8 family (Type B, two trips, 50 to 100 samples). The ECM reads the voltage across the injector enable and command wires and treats a pulse as undelivered when no opening magnitude shows up during catalyst heating.
s: Check engine light, frequently without driveability complaints
With a real injector fault, rough cold idle and possibly misfire on cylinder 8 (P0308)
c: Needle or armature of the cylinder 8 injector sticking on cold short pulses
Loose or corroded connector at injector 8
Chafed injector harness on the bank carrying cylinder 8

P2B10.d: P2B10 means the engine control holds no valid learned offset for injector 1 – the correction of the opening time used for very small injection quantities has not been established. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp, otherwise often no noticeable effect
Possibly harder combustion noise at idle on cylinder 1
c: Learn values cleared – after replacing injector 1 or the control unit, or after an adaption reset with a scan tool
Too few coasting phases with fuel cut-off for the learn to run
Injector 1 opening inconsistently, so no stable value is found

P2B11.d: P2B11 says the learned small-quantity correction for injector 1 has drifted beyond what the engine control may apply. Ford documents the code for its 3.0 L and 6.7 L Power Stroke diesels under Zero Fuel Calibration: the PCM fires a tiny test injection, compares the energising time that produced a measurable effect with the target stored for that injector and sets the code when the result is at least 156 µs too short
s: Check engine light
Diesel knock at idle, sometimes together with balance code P0263
c: Incorrectly learned injector values in the PCM (Ford TSB 18-2015, reset and reprogramming)
Injector 1 worn or coked so its opening behaviour has really shifted
Disturbed crankshaft speed signal falsifying the learn result

P2B12.d: P2B12 is stored when injector 2's pulse offset has not been learned, so the controller still relies on a default value for the smallest injections. The public record contains no manufacturer using this exact code; the explanation here follows from the title and from the neighbouring monitors.
s: Warning lamp without a clear driveability complaint
Possibly louder combustion on cylinder 2 at low load
c: Driving profile without enough fuel cut-off phases (constant load, towing)
Adaption values reset after work on injector 2 or the fuel system
Crankshaft speed signal too noisy to detect the test injection

P2B13.d: P2B13 concerns injector 2 on Ford's Power Stroke diesels: its zero-fuel learn value has run past the permitted band. Ford's 2023 OBD summary shows when the learn runs: continuously, typically within about 30 s, with coolant of at least 50 °C, intake air between 0 and 75 °C, fuel of at least 10 °C, at least 10 V supply, almost no pedal (up to 2 %) and rail pressure within 50 bar of its target.
s: Check engine light
Often no running fault; with a worn injector, knocking or rough idle
c: Steering wheel oscillation disturbing the crank or cam signal (Ford SSM 48877)
Injector 2 with genuinely shifted opening time due to wear or deposits
Implausible learned values in the PCM

P2B14.d: P2B14 tells that no offset has yet been learned for injector 3. No carmaker publishes this code for a specific engine, and the GM and Ford tables checked do not contain it.
s: Warning lamp, driving behaviour mostly unchanged
Slightly uneven idle in some cases
c: Learn not yet completed for all rail pressure levels of injector 3
Injector 3 or control unit recently replaced without completing the learn
Rail pressure not holding steady enough during the test injection

P2B15.d: P2B15 reports that the zero-fuel correction learned for injector 3 has reached Ford's limit. For its 3.0 L six-cylinder diesel Ford adds conditions so the test injection takes place in a defined overrun: engine speed between 890 and 2,400 rpm, a gear from fourth to tenth held without shifting, the torque converter locked and the fuel balance wheel learn already finished.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Possibly knocking or rough running at idle
c: Learned values unsuitable after fuel system repairs (Ford TSB 23-2076, software and adaption reset)
Injector 3 drifted mechanically (wear, coking, internal leakage)

P2B16.d: P2B16 indicates a missing learned pulse offset for injector 4. Public manufacturer material does not tie it to any engine; Ford's published diesel monitor and its bulletins use only the exceeded-limit partner P2B17.
s: Warning lamp
Louder combustion noise, especially at idle
c: Injector 4 or PCM replaced, or adaptions reset, and the learn not yet completed
Learn conditions (warm engine, fuel cut-off) rarely reached
Injector 4 not opening on minimal pulses at all

P2B17.d: P2B17 is set when injector 4's learned pulse offset goes past the allowed band. For the 6.7 L engine in 2020–2022 F-Super Duty trucks Ford saw this after fuel system work: stored learned values no longer matched the new parts.
s: Check engine light shortly after a fuel system repair
Usually unchanged driving behaviour
c: Old learn values after fuel system work, cleared by a warm idle relearn (Ford SSM 50646/50816)
Rail pressure deviating from target during the test injection

P2B18.d: P2B18 means injector 5 has no learned offset. No manufacturer documents this exact code.
s: Warning lamp
Rarely noticeable; at most slightly uneven low-load running
c: New injector 5 or control unit without a completed learn
Enabling conditions for the learn not met often enough
Faulty injector 5 wiring preventing a valid measurement

P2B19.d: P2B19 flags injector 5: its learned zero-fuel offset exceeds the calibrated limit. Ford's diesel OBD summary groups the code with the other odd numbers from P2B11 to P2B1F under the Zero Fuel Calibration monitor, which it files under fuel system feedback control.
s: Check engine light after mountain or high-plateau driving
Possibly slightly rough idle
c: Learned values skewed by driving above about 760 m (Ford SSM 53340)
PCM software without the later calibration fix

P2B1A.d: P2B1A reports that the pulse offset for injector 6 has not been learned. Public manufacturer sources do not name this code; on the 3.0 L V6 Power Stroke built by Ford, where cylinder 6 is the last one, Ford's summary lists only the exceeded-limit code P2B1B.
s: Warning lamp
Perhaps slightly harder combustion noise at idle
c: Learn for injector 6 still pending after a reset or parts replacement
Mostly short trips with a cold engine, so the learn rarely starts
Injector 6 delivering so erratically that no value can be fixed

P2B1B.d: P2B1B concerns injector 6. On Ford's 3.0 L V6 Power Stroke it is the last cylinder the zero-fuel monitor checks, on the 6.7 L V8 the sixth of eight.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly rough idle, driveability otherwise normal
c: PCM software learning wrong values at altitude (Ford TSB 25-2262)
Injector 6 drifted by wear or deposits
Adaptions not reset after an earlier repair

P2B1C.d: P2B1C says no learned offset exists for injector 7, which only applies to engines with at least seven cylinders, in practice V8s. No manufacturer publishes a monitor for this code.
s: Warning lamp
With an erratic injector, uneven idle or knocking on one cylinder
c: Test results for injector 7 scattering too much to be accepted
Learn restarted after injector or control unit replacement
Leak in the high-pressure system disturbing the test injection

P2B1D.d: P2B1D reports that the correction learned for injector 7 during Ford's zero-fuel calibration has gone beyond its limit; cylinder 7 exists only on the 6.7 L V8. Ford's TSB 25-2412 for 2023–2025 F-Super Duty trucks calls the warning lamp in many such cases incorrect: learned values skewed by operation above 762 m, sometimes with a slightly uneven idle.
s: Check engine light, sometimes without a real fault
Slightly uneven idle
c: Calibration learning wrong values at altitude (Ford TSB 25-2412)
Injector 7 worn, often with balance code P0281 as well
Interference on the crank or cam speed signal

P2B1E.d: P2B1E means injector 8 has not received a learned pulse offset. As the final cylinder in the group it belongs to V8 engines; Ford's 6.7 L V8 would be the obvious candidate, but Ford publishes only the exceeded-limit code P2B1F for it, so no manufacturer source for P2B1E exists.
s: Warning lamp
Mostly no noticeable change in running
c: Learn values reset or injector 8 replaced, learn not finished
Few coasting phases with fuel cut-off in everyday use
Fault in the crank speed signal or the injector 8 wiring

P2B1F.d: P2B1F is the last code of the series: the offset learned for injector 8 has crossed the learning limit. Ford uses it on the 6.7 L V8 Power Stroke.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly rough idle in some cases, otherwise normal running
c: Adaption skewed by high-altitude driving (Ford SSM 53896, reset with FDRS)

P2B20.d: Sensor B is a second temperature sensor in the coolant loop that serves the hybrid or EV power electronics, such as inverter, DC/DC converter or on-board charger; where it sits relative to sensor A is up to the vehicle maker. P2B20 is the undifferentiated circuit code: the controller finds the signal unusable without deciding between low and high.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and stored fault code
Reduced drive or charging power as a precaution
Electronics coolant pump running more often or at higher speed
c: Loose connector, corroded pins or broken wire in the sensor B circuit
Sensor B element open or shorted internally
Faulty input stage or reference supply in the controlling module

P2B21.d: Here sensor B delivers a voltage inside its electrical window, yet the temperature it reports does not fit the rest of the vehicle: it may stay flat while the electronics warm up, or disagree with other temperatures after the car has stood for hours. No manufacturer publishes the set condition of P2B21.
s: Hybrid system warning, often only after a cold start
Cooling pump or fan behaviour that does not match conditions
Occasionally limited electric power
c: Sensor B element drifted out of its characteristic curve
Air pocket around the sensor after coolant service or a leak
Corroded or loose terminals adding resistance to the signal
Controller calibration that needs an update

P2B22.d: P2B22 says the signal voltage of electronics coolant sensor B has fallen below its valid band. Since these sensors are NTC thermistors, a low voltage would mean an absurdly hot coolant, so the usual explanation is a signal wire touching ground, moisture bridging the connector or an internally shorted element.
s: Warning lamp or hybrid system message
Electronics coolant pump and fans running at high output
Reduced electric drive or charging power
c: Sensor B signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water or coolant in the sensor connector

P2B23.d: With P2B23 the signal of electronics coolant sensor B climbs close to the reference voltage. For an NTC sensor that reads as extreme cold, which in practice nearly always points to an interruption: an unplugged or water-damaged connector, a broken signal or ground lead, an open element, or more rarely a short to a voltage source.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning with MIL
Coolant temperature for sensor B shown at about −40 °C in live data
Power reduced as a precaution
c: Open signal or ground wire, or connector not fully seated
Water intrusion and corroded pins in a connector of the sensor circuit
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P2B24.d: Some electrified drivetrains measure the power electronics coolant at three points, for example ahead of the inverter, behind it and at the charger or DC/DC converter. P2B24 covers the third of these sensors, C, and reports a circuit fault the controller does not classify further.
s: Stored fault code, possibly with a hybrid system message
Lower charging or drive power in hot conditions
c: Connector or wiring fault in the sensor C circuit
Input stage of the evaluating module faulty

P2B25.d: P2B25 is the plausibility code for the third electronics coolant sensor. The signal is electrically sound, but its value cannot be right, for example because sensor C still reads cold while sensors A and B in the same loop have long warmed up, or because it jumps by an amount the coolant could not follow.
s: Fault code set after a cold start or a long drive
Cooling system reacting inconsistently
Possible limitation of charging power
c: Sensor C reading drifted away from the true temperature
Air in the loop or a weak pump leaving sensor C without flow
Corrosion in the sensor C connector

P2B26.d: The voltage on the signal line of sensor C, the third coolant sensor in the power electronics loop, is lower than the controller accepts. Low means voltage here, not temperature: on an NTC sensor it corresponds to an implausibly hot value.
s: Warning lamp or system message
Pump and radiator fan running hard even when cool
Reduced power in some situations
c: Sensor C signal lead pinched or chafed against ground
Coolant wicking into the sensor plug

P2B27.d: P2B27 is logged when sensor C in the power electronics coolant loop sends a signal near the top of the reference, which the controller would have to read as deep frost. Far more often than real cold, the reason is a circuit that has opened: a connector that has backed out, a terminal pushed out of its cavity, a broken wire near a moving part or a failed element; shorting to the battery feed is rarer.
s: Warning lamp and hybrid system message
Sensor C shown far below outside temperature in live data
Limited electric power
c: Connector backed out, terminal pushed out or wire broken
Signal line shorted to battery voltage

P2B28.d: P2B28 means battery coolant pump A is electrically reachable but does not perform as the battery controller expects. VW and Audi store P2B2800 in battery management J840: VW bulletin 93-21-02 (2021 ID.4) traces it to air left when pump V590 did not run during the fill-and-bleed routine, and Audi's 2068363 series (Q4 e-tron 2022–2024, message Electric drive fault) names dry running from residual air, prescribes two bl
s: Electric drive fault message or MIL
Reduced drive or charging power
Short or missing engine auto-stops on mild hybrids
c: Residual air in the battery coolant loop, often after service
Battery or hybrid controller software needing an update
Worn or failing battery coolant pump
Low coolant level from a leak

P2B29.d: A centrifugal pump that suddenly spins faster while drawing less current has lost its liquid: it is churning air. P2B29 reports exactly this for battery coolant pump A.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Pump audibly gurgling or whining
Battery power or charging limited
c: Air in the battery coolant loop after service or incomplete bleeding
Leak in a battery cooling line lowering the level
Battery controller software misjudging pump feedback (Ford 2020 hybrids)

P2B2A.d: The pump in the low-temperature loop that cools power electronics and often the drive unit reports that it is turning too fast for its load, the sign of air instead of coolant. Mercedes documents P2B2A7A in the powertrain control unit of the 167 series (GLE/GLS) with M177 V8 and 48 V system before model year 2024: the 15 W pump beside the transmission switches to an emergency dry-run mode when the circuit holds air,
s: Coolant or drive system warning in the instrument cluster
Churning noise from the affected pump
Reduced drive power until the loop is bled
c: Air in the low-temperature circuit after filling or a leak
Damaged or leaking coolant hose (Audi e-tron)
Pumps of the wrong part number or position (Mercedes 167)

P2B2B.d: Engines with split cooling, electric pumps or separate head, block, radiator and heater branches can carry five or more coolant sensors; the numbering is the maker's choice. P2B2B is the generic circuit code for number 5, meant for controllers that do not separate low from high.
s: MIL with stored code
Cooling fans or thermal management running on default values
c: Loose connector or broken lead at sensor 5
Faulty sensor input in the engine control module

P2B2C.d: P2B2C concerns a fifth coolant sensor whose signal is electrically valid but does not behave like coolant temperature: after a long cold soak it differs clearly from the other engine temperatures, it barely rises during warm-up although the engine heats normally, or it sits stuck at one value. CARB requires such rationality checks for coolant inputs that emission controls rely on.
s: MIL, often after a cold start
Heater or fan behaviour that does not match engine temperature
c: No coolant flow in the sensor's branch (stuck valve, failed pump, air)

P2B2D.d: A low signal from coolant sensor 5 means its NTC resistance has collapsed, which the engine computer would read as an impossibly hot engine; a grounded signal wire or a shorted element is the usual reason. GM documents P2B2D in its configurable temperature input system: the sensor 5 channel fails when its resistance drops below 47.5 Ω in the 2019 L3B tables or 55 Ω in the 2025 ECM tables, a value tied to roughly 150
s: MIL after two trips
Radiator fans running constantly at high speed
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time
c: Signal wire grounded, for example by a chafed harness

P2B2E.d: P2B2E is stored when the fifth coolant sensor shows a resistance so high that only an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a line shorted to voltage can explain it; the NTC curve would put the coolant below −60 °C. GM sets it once the channel exceeds about 298 kΩ in the 2019 L3B tables or about 174 kΩ in the 2025 ECM tables, for 5 s within 6 s, after an engine run time above 10 s or with intake air above −20 °C; T
s: MIL after two trips
Sensor 5 reads around −40 °C or lower in live data
Engine runs on a substitute temperature value
c: Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged connector
Chafed engine harness interrupting the circuit

P2B2F.d: Unlike the circuit codes P0480, P0691 and P0692, P2B2F judges the result: radiator fan 1 is commanded on but does not deliver, up to not turning at all. Detection uses fan speed feedback from a PWM or LIN fan module, or the missing temperature drop when the fan should be cooling.
s: MIL
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic
Weak air conditioning at standstill
c: Fan 1 motor worn or seized, or blades blocked by debris
Fan control module or relay not switching the motor
Engine software judging the fan wrongly (FCA 2.0 L)
Poor power feed or ground at the fan

P2B30.d: P2B30 states that radiator fan 1 does not follow the command to stop or to change speed, as judged from its speed feedback or module diagnosis. The classic electrical background is a welded relay contact or a fan module that keeps driving the motor.
s: Fan keeps running after switch-off, draining the 12 V battery
Weak cabin heating or cooling on electric vehicles
Grinding noise from the front wheel area
c: Road debris jamming the fan (Audi e-tron GT)
Fan control module ignoring the off command

P2B31.d: P2B31 is the functional code for a second radiator fan: its circuits test fine (otherwise P0481, P0693 or P0694 would be set), yet the fan turns too slowly or not at all when commanded. Twin-fan cooling packs usually run fan 2 for high load or A/C demand, so a failure tends to show up only in heat or traffic.
s: MIL or cooling warning
Temperature climbing at high load or with A/C on
c: Fan 2 motor worn, seized or jammed by debris
Fan module or relay for fan 2 not switching on
Weak supply or ground to fan 2

P2B32.d: With P2B32 the controller finds that the second radiator fan keeps operating, or does not change state, against its command. On conventional cars this usually traces back to a relay stuck closed, a fan 2 control line shorted to its active level or a module that has lost control of the motor.
s: Fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
Reduced heating, cooling or charging on electric vehicles
Flat 12 V battery after parking
c: Debris from the wheel housing jamming fan 2 (Audi e-tron GT)
Fan 2 control line shorted to its active level

P2B33.d: P2B33 concerns the second profile actuator on the intake camshaft (camshaft A) of bank 1. Such actuators are solenoids that extend a pin into a groove on a sliding cam sleeve and so move lobes of a different lift under the valves.
s: MIL on after the first drive with the fault
No change of intake lift profile, less pull or higher fuel use depending on the stuck profile
Cylinder deactivation no longer engages
c: Connector at the actuator on the camshaft carrier loose, corroded or not latched after valve cover work
Solenoid winding of actuator B open
Control wire broken in the engine harness
Output stage in the engine control module faulty

P2B34.d: On bank 1 the intake camshaft (A) carries a second shifting solenoid, actuator B, which GM's L3B 2.7-litre four labels actuator 2. P2B34 reports a short to ground on its control line: while the driver is switched on, the ECM measures 0.5 Ω or less from signal to ground and stores the fault after 4 failed out of 5 samples at more than 11 V, lighting the MIL at once (Type A).
s: MIL on, often together with other codes from the same harness section
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable
With a chafed harness also rough running, reduced power or blown fuses
c: Engine harness chafed through on the camshaft carrier or near the left shock tower (GM PIT5677)
Shorted turns or short to housing in actuator B
Oil or moisture in the actuator connector creating a path to ground

P2B35.d: P2B35 is the short-to-voltage counterpart for intake-side actuator B on bank 1, the second of the sleeve-shifting solenoids on camshaft A. In GM's L3B tables (2019 and again 2025) this test runs while the output is off: if the control line shows 0.5 Ω or less towards the controller supply, a short to power is assumed, and 4 hits in 5 samples set a Type A code with the warning lamp on in the same drive.
s: MIL on during the drive in which the fault appears
Intake lift profile no longer changes as commanded
Higher fuel use because cylinder deactivation is blocked
c: Control wire chafed against a powered circuit in the engine harness
Output stage in the engine control module faulty

P2B36.d: P2B36 describes an open control circuit at the second profile actuator of the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 2. A second bank exists only on V or boxer engines.
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 intake stays on one lift profile, possibly uneven running between the banks
c: Actuator connector on bank 2 unplugged, loose or corroded
Broken control wire between engine module and bank 2

P2B37.d: Code P2B37 stands for a control line shorted to ground at intake-side actuator B of bank 2, the second lobe-switching solenoid on camshaft A of the other cylinder bank. Publicly, no maker assigns it to a vehicle.
s: Check engine light on
Lift switching inactive on bank 2, less power or more fuel use
c: Harness to the bank 2 actuator chafed through on the cylinder head or a bracket
Oil or water in the actuator connector

P2B38.d: P2B38 marks a short to battery voltage in the control circuit of intake camshaft actuator B on bank 2. No published manufacturer documentation uses it; only the bank 1 version P2B35 is covered, by GM's L3B summary tables, which check with the output off and react to 0.5 Ω or less towards supply.
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 intake lift no longer changes, uneven power delivery
c: Pinched or chafed control wire touching a powered circuit
Faulty output stage in the engine module

P2B39.d: Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft, and actuator B is the second shifting solenoid on it. On GM's 2.7-litre L3B the exhaust side has only two such actuators, so this is the last of them; GM's tables call it exhaust camshaft profile actuator 2.
s: MIL on in the first drive
Exhaust lift profile no longer switches, cylinder deactivation unavailable
c: Exhaust actuator connector loose or corroded on the camshaft carrier
Broken wire in the engine harness
Open solenoid coil in exhaust actuator B

P2B3A.d: P2B3A points to a short to ground in the control line of exhaust-side actuator B on bank 1, i.e. the second pin solenoid that slides the lobe sleeve along camshaft B.
s: Check engine light on immediately
Exhaust profile and cylinder deactivation no longer switch
With harness damage often further codes and rough running
c: Engine harness rubbed through where it crosses the camshaft carrier
Shorted turns in exhaust actuator B
Oil wicking into the actuator connector

P2B3B.d: For the second exhaust-camshaft profile actuator on bank 1 (camshaft B, actuator B), P2B3B means its control circuit is shorted to a voltage source. GM's L3B strategy checks this with the driver switched off: a resistance of no more than 0.5 Ω between the line and controller power counts as a fault, and four out of five such readings at a supply above 11 V store a Type A code, MIL on at once.
s: Check engine light comes on during the drive
Exhaust lift stays in one profile, cylinder deactivation blocked
c: Control wire chafed against a live wire in the engine harness
Internal short in exhaust actuator B

P2B3C.d: This code reports an interrupted control circuit at actuator B on the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) of bank 2. No vehicle manufacturer is known to use P2B3C in public documents.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift on bank 2 no longer switches
c: Connector of the bank 2 exhaust actuator unplugged or loose
Open coil in exhaust actuator B

P2B3D.d: P2B3D: the control wire of the second exhaust-side profile actuator on bank 2 (camshaft B, actuator B) has contact with ground. Publicly documented use by a manufacturer is not known.
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 exhaust stays on one lift profile
c: Wire chafed at a bracket or valve cover edge on bank 2
Shorted coil in exhaust actuator B
Oil or water in the connector

P2B3E.d: P2B3E is set when the control circuit of exhaust camshaft profile actuator B on bank 2 is shorted to supply voltage. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, so the details come from the analogue: GM's L3B tests the bank 1 counterpart P2B3B while the output is off and treats 0.5 Ω or less towards controller power as a short.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift on bank 2 fixed, slightly higher consumption
c: Damaged insulation bringing the control wire against a powered line
Solenoid in exhaust actuator B shorted internally
Output stage in the engine module faulty

P2B3F.d: P2B3F is the general circuit code for position sensor B of the intake camshaft actuator (camshaft A) on bank 1, the side with cylinder 1; the NTN-SNR sensor guide also places it on the inlet side. Mercedes-Benz uses this code family on its M176/M177 V8 engines, where each CAMTRONIC lift actuator reports its own sensor signal and sensor B belongs to solenoid 2.
s: Check engine light on
Lift switching or cylinder deactivation unavailable
Slightly higher consumption, sometimes less power
c: Connector at the actuator loose, corroded or wire broken
Position sensor in the actuator failed (actuator replacement)
Engine harness damaged by heat or chafing

P2B40.d: With P2B40 the wiring of the intake-side sensor B (camshaft A, bank 1) is electrically fine, but its signal does not fit what the engine module commanded. Engines with switchable cam lift use such feedback to confirm that a pin really moved; GM's L3B, as a comparable case under P2C06, logs a fault when the Hall feedback shows movement although no shift was requested, or when the extending, extended and retracted stat
s: Check engine light on
Valve-lift change held in a safe position
Uneven running when the system tries to switch
c: Actuator pin sluggish or sticking (wear, oil sludge)
Engine control software outdated (Mercedes CAMTRONIC update)
Sensor signal disturbed by loose contact
Cam sleeve or shift groove damaged

P2B41.d: P2B41 reports a voltage below the permitted window from sensor B, which watches the intake actuator of bank 1. That usually points to a grounded signal line or a sensor that has failed internally.
s: Check engine light on
Cam lift switching disabled
Possibly further codes from sensors on the same supply
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed harness)

P2B42.d: Here sensor B of the bank 1 intake actuator reports a value stuck above its upper limit. Typical reasons are an open sensor ground, a signal line touching 5 V or battery voltage, or a defective sensor.
s: Check engine light on
Intake lift change locked out
Usually no noticeable change in driving, sometimes reduced power
c: Sensor ground open or connector corroded
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage

P2B43.d: P2B43 covers the wiring of sensor B at the bank 2 intake actuator, i.e. on the cylinder bank without cylinder 1, so it only appears on V or boxer engines.
s: Check engine light on
Cylinder deactivation or lift change switched off
Possibly limp-home message of the valve-lift system
c: Harness near the bulkhead damaged by heat

P2B44.d: P2B44 is the one code of this group with a public manufacturer use. Mercedes-Benz bulletin LI05.20-P-080192 (January 2026) lists P2B4400 on M176/M177 V8 engines – AMG 63 models, S 580, G 550, GLS 580 – and reads it as an implausible sensor signal from CAMTRONIC solenoid 2 on the intake side of bank 2.
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC limp-home mode, cylinder deactivation off
Higher fuel consumption at part load
c: Engine control software needs the CAMTRONIC update (Mercedes)
Actuator of an older part number (Mercedes replaces it)

P2B45.d: P2B45 means the bank 2 intake actuator's position sensor B delivers an unusually low voltage – on bank 2, which a V engine places opposite cylinder 1. A grounded signal wire is the classic cause; an internally shorted sensor or a missing supply gives the same picture.
s: Check engine light on
Lift change on bank 2 stops working
Possibly limp-home message
c: Signal wire grounded through chafing or heat damage

P2B46.d: P2B46 flags a signal from position sensor B on the bank 2 intake camshaft actuator that is stuck too high. Most often the sensor has lost its ground, the signal line has contact with a supply line, or the sensor element itself has failed.
s: Check engine light on
Cam lift held in default position on bank 2
Slightly increased fuel consumption
c: Signal line in contact with a supply line
Sensor element in the actuator failed

P2B47.d: P2B47 moves the circuit fault to the exhaust side: it concerns position sensor B on the actuator of camshaft B, bank 1. NTN-SNR's supplier code list reads camshaft B as the outlet camshaft.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust cam lift change unavailable
Little change in driving behaviour
c: Connector unplugged or corroded, wire broken

P2B48.d: P2B48 is the plausibility code for sensor B at the bank 1 exhaust actuator (camshaft B): the circuit works, yet the reported position contradicts the command. Mercedes handles this fault type on its CAMTRONIC V8s for the exhaust sensor of solenoid 1 as P34BD and fixes it through software and newer actuators; P2B48 itself is not found in any public manufacturer source.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift switching held in one position
Possibly rough running during shift attempts
c: Actuator pin sticking from deposits or wear
Shift groove or cam sleeve damaged

P2B49.d: With P2B49 the module reads too low a signal from position sensor B at the exhaust camshaft actuator of bank 1. A short between signal line and ground, a sensor with an internal short or a missing feed are the usual suspects.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust cam lift change switched off
Occasionally further sensor codes

P2B4A.d: P2B4A says the position sensor B signal of the bank 1 exhaust camshaft actuator is above its limit. An interrupted sensor ground, a short to a voltage source or a failed sensor are typical.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift system kept in safe position
Usually unchanged driveability
c: Sensor ground interrupted or connector corroded
Signal line shorted to a voltage source

P2B4B.d: P2B4B is set when the circuit feeding the second position sensor (B) of the exhaust actuator on bank 2 is open or otherwise unusable. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two cylinder rows, such as the Mercedes M176/M177 V8, whose CAMTRONIC bulletin lists exhaust feedback faults on bank 2 for sensor A (P34C1, P34C2) but not for sensor B.
s: Check engine light on
Cylinder deactivation or exhaust lift change unavailable
Somewhat higher consumption
c: Plug or wires at the actuator open
Heat damage to the harness above the bulkhead
Sensor in the exhaust actuator failed

P2B4C.d: P2B4C stands for an implausible but electrically valid signal from the B sensor watching the exhaust actuator of bank 2. It is the exhaust-side mirror of P2B44, which Mercedes-Benz documents on CAMTRONIC V8s (M176/M177) for intake solenoid 2 of bank 2; for P2B4C itself there is no public manufacturer text.
s: Check engine light on
Lift system or cylinder deactivation in limp-home
Higher part-load consumption
c: Intermittent contact in the sensor signal

P2B4D.d: A too-low signal from position sensor B at the bank 2 exhaust camshaft actuator sets P2B4D. In practice this is a signal wire touching ground, a shorted sensor, or a sensor that gets no supply.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift change on bank 2 out of action
Possibly limp-home message of the lift system
c: Signal wire touching ground (heat or chafe damage)

P2B4E.d: P2B4E closes the group: the exhaust-side position sensor B of bank 2 sends a signal above its upper limit. Usually the sensor ground is open, the signal line is shorted to a supply, or the sensor is faulty.
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 runs on the default cam profile
Slightly higher fuel use
c: Signal line shorted to a supply

P2B4F.d: P2B4F covers the second profile actuator (B) on the intake camshaft of bank 1, a solenoid whose pin engages a groove on a sliding cam sleeve to change valve lift. Despite the title wording, GM's L3B 2.7-litre four (19OBDG03D, again in 25OBDG03B) uses it for the reverse case: a Hall element reports three pin states (extending 55, extended 45, retracted 68), and if the signal falls below 55 although no shift was comman
s: MIL on in the first drive with the fault
Intake lift switching locked out, less pull or higher consumption
Cylinder deactivation no longer available
c: Actuator B pin extends without a command (sticking solenoid, weak return spring)
Hall feedback of the actuator delivers wrong pin states
Shift groove on the cam sleeve worn so the pin is dragged out

P2B50.d: Bank 2 of a V-engine has its own intake camshaft (A), and P2B50 reports that the second profile actuator on it does not do its job or stays in the off position. Mercedes-Benz documents the code for the M176 and M177 V8 with CAMTRONIC (for example AMG C63, GLC63 and S 580 models): in topic LI05.20-P-080192 of January 2026, solenoid 2 for the intake side of bank 2 is described as faulty or jammed off, with fault type 0
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC lift switching inactive on bank 2, possibly limp-home mode of the system
Slightly uneven running or higher fuel use at part load
c: CAMTRONIC actuator of an older part number, superseded by Mercedes
Engine control software that needs the available update
Harness heat-damaged above the bulkhead near the windscreen
Actuator pin mechanically jammed in the retracted position

P2B51.d: On the exhaust camshaft (B) of bank 1 the second sliding-cam solenoid is monitored by P2B51. GM applies it to the L3B 2.7-litre turbo four, whose exhaust side carries two such actuators.
s: MIL on immediately (Type A)
Exhaust lift profile no longer changes, turbo response may feel different
Cylinder deactivation disabled
c: Exhaust actuator B pin releases without command, often heat-related sticking
Faulty Hall feedback in the actuator or its signal line
Sludge or debris at the actuator bore hindering the pin

P2B52.d: P2B52 is the bank 2 version for actuator B on the exhaust camshaft (B): the second shifting solenoid either does not move its cam sleeve or remains in the off position. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift switching inactive on bank 2
Possibly slightly lower power in the upper speed range
c: Actuator B of the bank 2 exhaust camshaft does not extend its pin
Poor contact at the actuator connector or heat-damaged harness
Engine control calibration that judges the shift too strictly

P2B53.d: P2B53 means actuator B of the bank 1 intake camshaft is caught in the engaged position. GM documents it for the L3B 2.7-litre four as pin stuck: after a shift the Hall feedback must climb back above the retracted level of 68; if extending (55) or extended (45) was seen but the pin never reports home before the engine cycle ends, the ECM logs a stuck-out pin.
s: MIL on in the first drive
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation locked out
With a damaged harness also other codes, rough running or blown fuses
Possible ticking from the valve cover if the pin rubs in the groove
c: Actuator pin does not retract (sticking plunger, varnish, weak spring)
Engine harness chafed on the camshaft carrier (GM PIT5677 / 21-NA-149)
Hall feedback does not report the home position although the pin is back

P2B54.d: With P2B54 actuator B, the second shifter on the bank 2 intake camshaft, is reported as stuck on, meaning its pin or valve stays engaged after the command to release. A public manufacturer description of this exact code was not found.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running between the banks, especially at part load
Profile switching disabled by the engine control
c: Actuator B on the bank 2 intake camshaft stays engaged (sticking plunger)
Control line shorted so the solenoid remains energised
Position feedback of the actuator stuck at the engaged value

P2B55.d: P2B55 flags actuator B on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft as stuck on. Even GM, whose L3B four has a second exhaust actuator and uses P2B51 for it, lists no stuck-on code for that actuator in its 2019 and 2025 tables; no other maker documents P2B55 publicly either.
s: Check engine light on
Changed turbo response or reduced power
Possible metallic noise from the camshaft area
c: Pin of exhaust actuator B does not retract, often from heat and deposits
Solenoid stays powered because of a wiring or driver fault
Damaged shift groove holds the pin

P2B56.d: P2B56 completes the series: on bank 2 the second actuator of the exhaust camshaft remains engaged after it should have released. No manufacturer publishes a description of this exact code.
s: Check engine light on
Bank-to-bank imbalance felt as rough idle or part-load vibration
Lift switching locked by the engine control
c: Solenoid of exhaust actuator B on bank 2 sticking in the engaged state
Aged or wrong engine oil slowing the pin
Worn shift groove on the exhaust cam sleeve

P2B57.d: P2B57 is a status code rather than a circuit fault: the engine control has measured or calculated oil pressure too low for safe camshaft adjustment and has therefore switched the cam control off. Hydraulic cam phasers and oil-operated lift switching need a minimum pressure to hold position; below it the parts would rattle or drift.
s: Check engine light on, often together with an oil pressure warning
Camshaft adjustment inactive, weaker low-end torque and rough idle
Rattle from the cam phasers at start or when hot
c: Oil level too low or oil of the wrong viscosity
Worn oil pump, faulty pump control or clogged pickup screen
Oil pressure sensor reading too low although pressure is fine
Worn bearings causing internal oil leakage at high temperature

P2B58.d: P2B58 reports that the electric motor driving the engine coolant flow control valve draws too much current. GM documents the check for its 3.0-litre inline-six Duramax diesel: in the 2025 table 25OBDG04B the driver stage flags a current above 5.5 A, and 80 failures in 100 samples taken every 12.5 ms set a Type B fault, so the MIL follows on the second trip.
s: MIL on after the second drive with the fault
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
Fans may run more often as a precaution
c: Rotary valve stiff or seized from deposits or debris in the housing
Chafed engine harness on GM LM2 (bulletin 21-NA-149)

P2B59.d: P2B59 is the open-circuit check for the drive of the coolant flow control valve. In GM's 25OBDG04B (3.0 L Duramax) the driver reports a load resistance above 200 kΩ, meaning one of the motor wires is disconnected; 80 of 100 samples set a Type B fault.
s: MIL on, often without any noticeable driveability change
Valve stays in its default position, slower warm-up possible
c: ECU judgement logic on Hyundai/Kia 2.5 Theta III (software update 26-EM-009H / ENG 264)
Valve connector unplugged, loose or with a pushed-out terminal
Motor wire broken in the harness or valve motor winding open

P2B5A.d: P2B5A stands for a short to ground in the control wiring of the coolant flow control valve motor. GM's 2025 table for the 3.0-litre Duramax describes the detection: the driver sees more than 9 A flowing, which it interprets as one motor wire touching ground, and 80 out of 100 samples at 12.5 ms set a two-trip Type B fault once relay voltage exceeds 11 V.
s: MIL on after two drives
Engine temperature control fixed, slower warm-up or higher running temperature
c: Motor wire chafed or pinched against ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short to housing in the valve motor

P2B5B.d: P2B5B covers a short to battery voltage on the motor leads of the coolant flow control valve. GM's diesel table 25OBDG04B evaluates it through the driver stage as well: a current above 9 A with a lead tied to supply counts as a failure, and the usual 80-of-100 rule with 12.5 ms sampling stores a Type B code.
s: MIL on after two drives, possibly further codes from the same harness
Blown fuses or rough running if the harness is chafed
Weak heater output during warm-up
c: Motor lead chafed against a powered circuit (GM LM2, 21-NA-149)
Corroded or wet connector bridging to supply
Driver stage in the engine control module faulty

P2B5C.d: With P2B5C the supply voltage reaching the driver of the coolant flow control valve motor is too low. GM monitors this on the 3.0-litre Duramax (25OBDG04B): if the motor driver sees less than 6 V while the powertrain relay delivers more than 11 V, the difference points at the feed path, and a Type B fault follows after 80 hits in 100 samples.
s: MIL on after two drives
Valve does not move, temperature control in fallback mode
c: Blown or loose fuse, corroded relay contact in the valve feed
Supply wire damaged or chafed in the engine harness
High resistance at a ground or splice of the feed circuit

P2B5D.d: P2B5D is the general circuit code for the position sensor of the coolant flow control valve, the feedback that tells the engine computer how far the rotary valve has turned. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Check engine light on
Coolant flow control in fallback, warm-up or heating behaviour changed
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the valve connector
Signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor interrupted
Position sensor inside the valve faulty

P2B5E.d: P2B5E reports a position sensor reading below its valid window. On GM's 3.0-litre Duramax the valve sends its angle as a raw SENT value in percent of 5 V; anything under 2 % counts as too low, and 80 failures in 100 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B fault, provided there is no SENT communication fault and the relay supplies more than 11 V.
s: MIL on after two drives
Coolant flow no longer regulated, warm-up slower
c: 5 V reference or signal wire interrupted or shorted to ground
Chafed engine harness on GM LM2 (21-NA-149)
Position sensor in the valve faulty

P2B5F.d: P2B5F is set when the valve position signal sits above the top of its window. The 2025 Duramax calibration (3.0 L, 25OBDG04B) treats a SENT raw value over 98 % of 5 V as implausibly high and stores a two-trip Type B code after 80 of 100 readings, sampled every 6.25 ms while the SENT link itself is healthy.
s: MIL on after two drives
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging contacts in the valve connector
Position sensor in the valve faulty

P2B60.d: P2B60 checks whether the valve actually goes where it is told. On GM's 3.0 L Duramax the code sets when the gap between desired and measured position exceeds 12 % in 160 of 200 samples, only with a steady command, closed-loop control active and no coolant or outside temperature sensor fault (Type B).
s: MIL on after two drives
Engine temperature fluctuates or warms up slowly
Often no driveability complaint beyond the warning lamp
c: Engine control software (GM 20-NA-039 / 22-NA-082, Hyundai/Kia ITM logic)
Corroded terminals at the valve actuator connector (GM PIP5764)
Valve sluggish or not learned, needs a relearn after test
Valve does not follow commands although wiring is fine

P2B61.d: P2B61 indicates that the coolant flow control valve stays closed although the engine computer asks it to open, so coolant cannot reach the radiator path as intended. Jaguar Land Rover uses it on the 2.0-litre Ingenium petrol four (2019–2020): in bulletin JLRTB02030NAS1, P2B61-73 appears with P26CB-72 when the movable shroud that diverts coolant in the electrically controlled pump stays put, and the PCM runs the fans
s: Radiator fans running constantly at high speed, loud noise from the engine bay
Rising engine temperature under load
Check engine light on
c: Valve or diversion shroud mechanically stuck closed (JLR variable coolant pump)
Engine control software that needs an update
Valve drive or its wiring no longer moves the valve

P2B62.d: P2B62 flags a supply voltage problem at coolant pump B, an electrically driven auxiliary pump with its own electronics. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary files it as failure type 1C (supply voltage outside its permitted band) under base code P261A, in the check of pump B, which Ford defines as the high-temperature-loop auxiliary pump for component cooling #1.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Auxiliary pump runs slowly or not at all
Rising temperature of the component cooled by pump B
c: Pump fuse blown or supply relay not closing properly
Corroded or loose power or ground connection at the pump
Weak battery or charging system fault lowering supply voltage
Voltage detection inside the pump electronics faulty

P2B63.d: P2B63 means coolant pump B is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn, or stays far below target speed. Brushless auxiliary pumps notice this themselves, for example from high current without rotation, and report it to the engine computer.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
No audible pump run after the ignition is switched on
Overheating of the component served by pump B
c: Bearing seized or impeller jammed by debris or deposits
Electric motor or electronics inside the pump failed
Coolant frozen in the pump because antifreeze concentration is too low

P2B64.d: P2B64 reports that the electronics built into coolant pump B have become too hot and the pump has protected itself, usually by derating or shutting down. In Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary it is failure type 98 (system over temperature) of the pump B check under P261A, monitored continuously.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump stops intermittently, often after long or hot drives
Reduced cooling of the served component
c: Coolant level low or air at the pump, so the electronics are not cooled
Sluggish impeller raises motor current and heat
Power stage inside the pump degraded
Damaged heat shield or high radiant heat at the mounting point

P2B65.d: When a coolant pump draws in air, its impeller loses load: speed climbs and current drops. P2B65 reports this for coolant pump B.
s: Coolant or overheating warning in the instrument cluster
Falling coolant level in the expansion tank
Gurgling noise or fluctuating temperature display
c: Air left in the circuit after filling or repair
Coolant loss through a leak, level too low
Restricting check valve in the vent hose (Bentley W12, 975 122 447H)
Speed or current detection inside the pump faulty

P2B66.d: P2B66 is the open-circuit code for the control line of coolant pump D, the pump a manufacturer labels D in its thermal management. The driver stage in the engine computer detects a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a pump input that no longer draws current.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D does not respond to commands
Higher temperature in the loop served by pump D
c: Pump connector loose, corroded or unplugged
Control wire broken between engine computer and pump
Control input inside the pump open

P2B67.d: P2B67 means the control line of coolant pump D sits too low, typically because it is shorted to ground or the driver stage sees excess current. No manufacturer publishes this code.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D runs constantly or not at all
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the pump connector
Control input inside the pump shorted

P2B68.d: P2B68 flags a control line for coolant pump D that reads too high: it touches a voltage source or is pulled up while the driver should switch it. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D runs at a fixed speed or ignores commands
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
Fault in the pump electronics pulls the line up

P2B69.d: P2B69 reports that coolant pump D does not receive a usable voltage on its power feed, as distinct from the control line covered by P2B66 to P2B68. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D slow or inactive
Code returns mainly at low battery voltage or high electrical load
c: Fuse blown or supply relay contacts worn
High resistance at the pump ground or ground point

P2B6A.d: P2B6A reports that coolant pump D is blocked or stalled: supply and command are present, yet the rotor does not come up to speed. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D silent although commanded
Overheating of the loop served by pump D
c: Bearing seized or impeller jammed by debris or sludge
Motor winding or pump electronics failed
Coolant frozen because antifreeze concentration is too low

P2B6B.d: With P2B6B the integrated electronics of coolant pump D report excessive temperature, and the pump derates or switches itself off to survive. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the equivalent for pump B is P2B64, which Ford lists as failure type 98 (system over temperature), and for pump A it is P2B9E.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D cuts out after longer operation and restarts after cooling
c: Too little coolant or air at the pump
Power stage inside the pump degraded

P2B6C.d: P2B6C means coolant pump D is spinning faster than its command would explain, the signature of an impeller moving air instead of liquid. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Coolant warning or rising temperature display
Gurgling from the cooling circuit
Coolant level drops in the expansion tank
c: Circuit not fully bled after filling or repair
Vent line or bleed valve restricted, air cannot escape

P2B6D.d: P2B6D covers a position signal from the engine coolant flow control valve that drops out or jumps for short moments, even though single readings may still lie inside the valid window. This exact code appears in no public manufacturer document.
s: Warning lamp, code often stored as intermittent
Temperature display or warm-up behaviour fluctuates
c: Loose or widened terminal in the valve connector
Fretting corrosion on the signal or reference pins
Harness rubbing or flexing with engine movement
Position sensor inside the valve unstable

P2B6E.d: P2B6E is the general circuit code for temperature sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger. SAE J2012 names the sensor but leaves its measuring point open, so the manufacturer decides what it watches, and no manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Implausible or jumping turbo temperature value in live data
c: Intermittent break in signal or ground wire

P2B6F.d: P2B6F reports that the signal of turbocharger/supercharger temperature sensor A has fallen below its valid range. If the sensor is an NTC thermistor, whose resistance drops as it warms, a low voltage stands for a very high temperature, so the usual electrical causes are a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor failed internally short.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Live data shows an extreme value even with the engine cold
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, for example chafed near the exhaust
Input circuit in the engine computer faulty

P2B70.d: P2B70 is set when sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger delivers a signal above its valid range. For an NTC thermistor this corresponds to an implausibly cold reading, the classic result of an open signal or ground wire, an unplugged connector or a short to the 5 V reference; for a PTC-type element it would indicate extreme heat.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Live data shows a fixed extreme value
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector unplugged
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or another voltage

P2B71.d: P2B71 covers a reading from temperature sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger that is electrically valid yet does not fit the operating state. Typical plausibility tests compare the value after a long engine-off soak with other temperature sensors, or check it against a model; Cummins patent US8082736B2 shows how a turbine-side temperature can be derived from pressure signals, which gives the computer such a r
s: Warning lamp, often without noticeable driving change
Turbo temperature in live data differs clearly from other temperatures after a cold start
Boost may be trimmed back as a precaution
c: Sensor element aged by heat and reading off
Contact resistance at the connector distorting the signal
Sensor loose or not fully seated in its bore

P2B72.d: P2B72 says the command line to coolant heater A is open or has lost continuity. Keep it apart from the engine coolant heater family P01E8–P01EF: the other J2012 codes for this heater – internal module, supply voltage and over-temperature under P2DA4–P2DA7, lost communication under U069E – point to a unit with its own electronics, such as the electric coolant heater of hybrids and EVs.
s: Little or no cabin heat, especially in electric driving
Engine starts more often in cold weather to provide heat (hybrids)
Warning or fault message, depending on the manufacturer
c: Command wire to the heater broken or connector not latched
Terminal pushed back or corroded in the heater connector
Input stage of the heater electronics open internally
Output stage in the commanding control module faulty

P2B73.d: P2B73 is the low case on the command circuit of coolant heater A: the commanding module reads the line at or near ground when it expects a higher level. Usual reasons are a chafed wire touching body ground, coolant or water in a connector, or an input in the heater that pulls the line down.
s: Coolant heater does not switch on, weak cabin heat
Engine runs more often in the cold (hybrids)
Fuse for the request circuit may blow repeatedly
c: Command wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the heater connector
Input of the heater electronics shorted internally
Commanding module cannot drive the line high

P2B74.d: P2B74 is the opposite of P2B73: the command circuit of coolant heater A sits at or near supply voltage while the module expects it low, or the output stage measures excess current and shuts down. A wire rubbed through onto a 12 V feed, a crushed harness next to the heater's own supply cable or a shorted input in the heater electronics are typical.
s: Coolant heater off, or running without request
Higher 12 V or high-voltage battery drain when parked if the heater runs on
Weak cabin heat in cold weather
c: Command wire shorted to a 12 V circuit
Harness crushed or melted near the heater supply cable
Heater electronics input shorted to its supply
Output stage of the commanding module faulty

P2B75.d: P2B75 is set when the command circuit of coolant heater A tests electrically sound but the heater's response does not match the request – the coolant leaving it fails to warm, for instance, or reported power or current stays off target. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.2) asks for this kind of functional check on output components.
s: Cabin warms slowly or only with the engine running
Heater core temperature in live data stays low despite full heat request
Electric range reduced in winter because the engine starts for heat
c: Air trapped in the heater loop or low coolant level
Heating element weak or partly failed
Internal fault in the heater control electronics
Coolant pump or valve in the heater loop not circulating enough

P2B76.d: P2B76 reports an open command circuit for coolant heater B. Where a vehicle has two separately requested heaters or heating stages – Hyundai and Kia patent US11378000B2 describes one housing with several sheath elements that a controller switches individually – B stands for the second channel.
s: Reduced heating power, cabin warms more slowly
Defrosting takes longer in cold weather
Fault entry often without other noticeable effects
c: Request wire for heater B broken at a flex point
Terminal pushed out of the heater connector
Fuse feeding the request circuit blown
Heater B input open inside the heater electronics

P2B77.d: P2B77 means the command circuit of coolant heater B reads low: the line is pulled toward ground although the module drives or expects a higher level. With a second heating stage this usually costs part of the heating power rather than all of it, because stage A can still run.
s: Heating power noticeably lower than usual
Cabin and windows take longer to warm up
Possible traces of coolant at the heater connector
c: Harness branch along the coolant hoses shorted to ground
Coolant seepage corroding the heater connector
Heater B input shorted inside the heater electronics

P2B78.d: P2B78 flags the command line of coolant heater B as too high: voltage is present where the commanding module expects a low level, or its driver reports overcurrent. A short to a 12 V circuit is the classic cause; with a low-side driver, a heater input that has failed short can produce it as well.
s: Heater stage B off, or running although not requested
Unusual battery drain while parked
Lower heating power in winter
c: Request wire for heater B shorted to a 12 V circuit
Heater B input failed short inside the heater
Damage in a harness section shared with heater A

P2B79.d: P2B79 says that coolant heater B is wired correctly but does not do what it is told: after a request the expected warming, current or status feedback fails to appear. In layouts with several stages, as in Hyundai and Kia patent US11378000B2, the controller switches the stages individually and shuts them down when outlet or housing surface temperature runs too high – a stage disabled by that protection can look like a
s: Heating power lower than expected
Heater outlet temperature rises slowly in live data
Fault may only appear at low outside temperatures
c: Low coolant or trapped air, so protection shuts the stage down
Heating element of stage B weak or open
Internal fault in the heater electronics for stage B

P2B7A.d: P2B7A is the general circuit fault of a third EVAP pressure sensor or switch, C, alongside A (P0450 range) and B (P24D5 range). Each maker assigns the letters itself.
s: Check engine light on
EVAP readiness monitor stays incomplete
Usually no change in driving behaviour
c: Sensor of an early design (VW G400 with narrow orifice)
Open or short in reference, ground or signal wire
Control unit logs a wrong fault entry (Audi bulletin 2069531)

P2B7B.d: P2B7B means sensor C delivers a signal that is electrically valid but implausible. Mercedes-AMG documents it as P2B7B26 on the GT63 S E Performance (2024–2026): the ME control unit sees the signal change too slowly, caused by interference on the line, and bulletin LI07.70-P-078293 cures it by twisting the sensor leads that run between the engine computer and the EVAP sensors.
s: Check engine light on, no driveability complaint
EVAP readiness monitor not completing
Code returns after clearing, often after a few drives
c: Sensor port or orifice too narrow or blocked
Fault entry assigned to the wrong sensor (Audi bulletin 2069531)
Pressure sensor C drifting or sluggish

P2B7C.d: P2B7C reports that the signal of EVAP pressure sensor C stays below its valid voltage window. The only public manufacturer reference is VW: on the 2025–2026 Jetta (engine DNKA) and Taos FWD (DYBA) the code points to fuel tank pressure sensor G400 with its NVLD switch, and bulletin 01-26-01 replaces the sensor assembly with the revised plug housing (part 5WA201700B) if the old version is fitted.
s: Check engine light on
EVAP leak tests not carried out, readiness incomplete
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too
c: 5 V reference to the sensor missing or shorted

P2B7D.d: P2B7D is the high counterpart to P2B7C: the signal of EVAP pressure sensor C sits above its valid range. VW lists it in bulletin 01-26-01 for the 2025–2026 Jetta and Taos FWD, whose fuel tank pressure sensor G400 came with a plug-housing orifice that proved too small; the first step is to check which housing version is installed.
s: Check engine light on
EVAP readiness not set after clearing codes
Car usually drives normally
c: Sensor ground wire open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage

P2B7E.d: P2B7E covers a signal from EVAP pressure sensor C that drops out or jumps for brief moments instead of failing for good. No manufacturer documents P2B7E publicly; Audi and VW use only P2B7A and P2B7B, VW also P2B7C and P2B7D, for this sensor.
s: Check engine light comes and goes
Pressure reading jumps in live data
Fault often appears only on rough roads or in wet weather
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor connector
Harness chafing near the tank or along the underbody
Electrical interference on the signal line
Pressure sensor C with an intermittent internal fault

P2B7F.d: P2B7F applies where boost control A is handled by its own electronic module, typically a smart actuator on the charger, and that module reports missing or invalid calibration data. Honeywell patent US7689376B2 describes such a controller holding a multi-point calibration measured for its individual turbocharger, and Melett notes for REA-type actuators that this data is unique to each unit, so swapped or new parts mus
s: Warning lamp right after a repair on the turbo system
Reduced boost or emergency mode
c: New or used module or charger fitted without programming or learn routine
Programming aborted, for example by low battery voltage
Module has lost its stored calibration (internal fault)

P2B80.d: P2B80 is the counterpart of P2B7F for the second boost control module, which only exists where two chargers or two separately driven actuators each carry their own electronics. It is set when module B has no valid calibration or its learn step was never completed.
s: Warning lamp after work on the second charger
Reduced power because boost on one side is limited
c: Module B or its charger replaced without programming or learn routine
Modules or chargers fitted on the wrong side

P2B81.d: P2B81 reports that electric wastegate A does not behave as commanded although its sensor signal is electrically fine. GM documents it for the 2.7L L3B (table 19OBDG03D): with the actuator in normal operation the fault counts if the position error exceeds 20 % for over 1 s, actuator current exceeds 1.0 A for over 1 s or duty cycle exceeds 40 % for over 1 s, and 25 of 30 samples must fail; the 2025 table 25OBDG03B tigh
s: MIL in the first trip
Boost too low or too high, flat or jerky acceleration
Reduced power mode possible
c: Wastegate valve or linkage binding (GM PIP6007A, turbo replacement)
Electric wastegate actuator worn or drawing excessive current
Linkage clip missing or rod detached

P2B82.d: P2B82 is the performance fault for the second electric wastegate, found only on engines with two turbochargers and position-controlled wastegates. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Uneven or reduced boost, weaker pull
c: Wastegate valve B or linkage binding from heat and deposits
Actuator B worn, gear or motor weak

P2B83.d: P2B83 concerns the electric pump that keeps coolant moving through a water-cooled charge air cooler. When the impeller runs in air instead of liquid, load vanishes and the motor spins up.
s: Check engine light after two drives with the fault
Reduced power under load because the intake air gets hot
Falling level in the charge air cooler coolant reservoir
c: Air pocket in the charge air cooler loop after service or a leak
Low coolant level in the separate low-temperature loop
Impeller loose or broken on the pump shaft
Pump electronics reporting an implausible speed

P2B84.d: P2B84 reports that the electric charge air cooler pump is turning too slowly or not at all, judged by the speed its own electronics send back. GM lists the code next to P2B83 in the 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B as the low out-of-range case of the pump speed, with the limit printed as a reading below -115 rpm; 8 failed one-second samples out of 10 are needed, with the pump fitted and enabled, relay voltage at 11 V or m
s: Check engine light after the second faulty drive
Less power under heavy load or when towing
High charge air temperature shown in live data
c: Worn or seized pump bearing, or debris blocking the impeller
Water or corrosion in the pump connector
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
Pump motor or its electronics worn out

P2B85.d: P2B85 applies to engines whose main water pump is electric: the pump turns clearly slower than commanded. On GM's 2.7-litre L3B (table 19OBDG03D) the filtered gap between commanded and reported speed must exceed a map value – 200 rpm at low commands, up to 800 rpm at 8,000 rpm – during 8 of 10 seconds, with 300–6,250 rpm requested and more than 11 V; there it is Type A, MIL on the first trip, while the 2025 table 25O
s: Rising coolant temperature and overheating warnings
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
Check engine light, often on the first trip
Engine may be shut down if driving continues
c: Failed control board inside the electric water pump
Loose or poorly latched plug at the pump
Bearing wear or deposits slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or high resistance in power or ground

P2B86.d: P2B86 says coolant pump A spins faster than it was told to – the typical sign of air at the impeller. In GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) the filtered gap between command and feedback must stay beyond a map limit, the pump running 200 to 348 rpm too fast depending on the 300–3,480 rpm request, over 8 s of a 10 s span at more than 11 V; Type B.
s: Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Weak or fluctuating cabin heat
Coolant warning or gurgling noise in the heater area
c: Air trapped in the loop after a repair or incomplete bleeding
Coolant loss through a leak, low level in the reservoir
Foreign object such as a loose O-ring at the pump ports
Restricted bleed or vent hose keeping air in the system

P2B87.d: With P2B87 the reported speed of coolant pump A stays below the commanded one. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) compare filtered command and feedback against a calibrated limit while 300–3,480 rpm is requested and more than 11 V is present; 8 s in a 10 s window, Type B.
s: Check engine light, often without any other complaint
Reduced cabin heat at idle or with the engine stopped
c: Outdated software in the module that commands the pump
Impeller slowed by debris or a foreign O-ring
Worn bearing or motor in the auxiliary pump
Low voltage or poor contact at the pump connector

P2B88.d: P2B88 is the catch-all electrical code for the oxygen sensor that some turbocharged engines mount in the intake tract, behind compressor and charge air cooler, to judge how much exhaust the recirculation system is feeding back. Ford's patents describe this intake sensor as a heated wide-band element whose pumping current shrinks as recirculated gas dilutes the fresh charge.
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or switched off, with slightly higher fuel use or knock-limited power
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Corroded or loose sensor plug, often wetted by charge air cooler condensate
Open or chafed signal wire between sensor and engine module
Intake oxygen sensor element internally failed
Fault in the sensor input stage of the engine module

P2B89.d: With P2B89 the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor signal sits below the lowest voltage the engine module accepts. Typical electrical reasons are a signal lead shorted to ground, a damaged element or a corroded plug near the charge air cooler, where condensate gathers.
s: Check engine light on
EGR flow limited or disabled by the engine module
Other stored codes such as P2AC0 or P0402 on the same vehicle
c: Engine software detecting falsely (Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 EC2, fixed by reflash)
Signal wire shorted to ground or pinched in the harness
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector

P2B8A.d: P2B8A is the mirror image of P2B89: the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor delivers a voltage above its valid window. On a wide-band element this usually comes from a signal wire touching a supply or the heater feed, from an open ground or reference return that lets the input float upward, or from water inside the connector.
s: Check engine light on
EGR switched off, possibly slightly higher fuel consumption
Intake oxygen reading on the scan tool above the fresh-air value
c: Signal wire shorted to a supply or to the heater feed
Open ground or reference return lead of the sensor

P2B8B.d: P2B8B is about the heater of bank 1's intake oxygen sensor: the module switches the heater on but sees no current, the classic sign of a broken heater coil, an open feed or control lead, or a blown fuse in the heater supply. A wide-band sensor only measures once its ceramic is hot.
s: Check engine light on
EGR stays inactive because the intake sensor never becomes ready
Possible companion code for the sensor signal
c: Heater coil inside the sensor burnt through or cracked
Blown fuse or failed relay in the heater supply
Open heater feed or control wire, loose connector pin
Heater driver in the engine module failed
