P2B8C.d: P2B8C is not about broken wires: the heater of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor is electrically intact, yet the element does not reach or hold its temperature as expected, or the heater needs power that does not fit the conditions. Mounted right after the intercooler, this sensor gets hit by condensate.
s: Check engine light on
Fault often appears in humid or cold weather and with high boost
EGR temporarily reduced
c: Water from the charge air cooler reaching the hot sensor element
Heater aged with increased resistance, sensor slow to warm up
Corroded pins or high resistance in the heater supply
Low system voltage limiting heater power

P2B8D.d: P2B8D means the voltage the module sees on the heater control wire of bank 1's intake oxygen sensor is lower than the module expects for the commanded state, usually because the line is shorted to ground. Many engine modules switch such heaters on the ground side; there a control wire chafed against the body can keep the heater running even when it should be off, which overheats the ceramic and can crack it.
s: Check engine light on
Heater switched off by the module, EGR feedback unavailable
Repeated sensor failure if the short is not repaired
c: Heater control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Heater coil with shorted turns inside the sensor
Water bridging the heater pins in the connector
Heater output stage in the engine module defective

P2B8E.d: With P2B8E, bank 1's intake O2 heater control wire shows more voltage than expected, as when it is shorted to battery voltage or when the driver cannot pull it down. If the module switches the heater on its ground side, such a short means the heater never receives current, the element stays cold and the sensor is never released for measuring.
s: Check engine light on
Intake oxygen sensor stays cold and not ready
EGR inactive
c: Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Heater with too low resistance tripping the driver's overcurrent protection
Damaged connector with pins touching each other
Heater output stage in the engine module defective

P2B8F.d: P2B8F is the general circuit fault for temperature sensor B, the second sensor of this kind on a charged engine, often belonging to a second turbocharger. Which spot it watches is left to the manufacturer, and none documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Sensor B value missing or jumping in live data
c: Loose or heat-damaged connector with intermittent contact
Wiring chafed or brittle near hot exhaust parts

P2B90.d: P2B90 means the signal of temperature sensor B has dropped below the lowest value the engine computer accepts. What that says about temperature depends on the element: an NTC thermistor loses resistance when hot, so a low signal reads as extreme heat, whereas a platinum resistor of the kind Heraeus patented for turbo protection (US8328419B2) gains resistance with heat, so a low signal reads as extreme cold.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Sensor B shows a fixed extreme value even on a cold engine
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, for example melted insulation
Faulty input stage in the engine computer

P2B91.d: P2B91 is stored when temperature sensor B delivers a signal above its permitted window. By far the most frequent reason is a broken current path: an unplugged or corroded connector, a cracked wire or an element that has burned open, which pulls the input up to its reference voltage.
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Sensor B stuck at an end value in live data
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector unplugged or corroded
Sensor element or its lead wires broken by heat cycling
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage

P2B92.d: P2B92 says that temperature sensor B delivers a plausible voltage whose content is wrong: it may hang at one value, follow load changes too slowly or disagree with its partner sensor A on an engine with two chargers. A sensor that sits in a soot-coated or oil-wetted spot reacts sluggishly and is a classic trigger.
s: Warning lamp, usually without drivability change
Sensor B lags behind or contradicts sensor A in live data
Boost may be limited as a precaution
c: Sensor tip coated with soot or oil, responds sluggishly
Sensor element aged and reading off
Contact resistance in connector or wiring

P2B93.d: P2B93 concerns the learned closed position of electric wastegate A. The computer periodically drives the valve onto its seat and stores the sensor value found there; Ford's patent US9243553B2 explains why: linkage length drifts with temperature and the reference must be refreshed.
s: MIL in the first trip
Boost slightly low because the valve does not fully close
c: Wastegate linkage bent, stretched or wrongly adjusted
Wastegate flap or seat worn so the valve travels too far
Turbocharger or actuator replaced and relearn not completed

P2B94.d: P2B94 is set when the learned end position of electric wastegate B falls outside the window the engine computer accepts. Stellantis documents it on the 2025 Ram 1500 with the 3.0L Hurricane twin-turbo: bulletin 09-008-25 (Rev.
s: MIL on, often together with P0248
Lack of acceleration from the turbo
c: Wastegate rod retention clips incorrectly installed (Stellantis 09-008-25)
Play or bending in the wastegate B linkage
Charger or actuator B replaced without completed relearn

P2B95.d: P2B95 belongs to the cold-start strategy of petrol direct-injection engines: while the catalyst is heated, each injection is split into two or more small pulses, and the module checks via the injector coil voltage that every pulse really opened the injector. Unlike P2B08 to P2B0F, which name a cylinder, P2B95 is the engine-wide verdict.
s: Check engine light after two cold starts with the fault
Usually no noticeable effect on driving
Possibly rough running in the first seconds after a cold start
c: Engine software setting the code falsely (GM and Stellantis reflash bulletins)
Injector opening sluggishly when cold due to deposits or wear
High resistance or chafing in injector wiring
Rail pressure outside the expected range during cold start

P2B96.d: P2B96 is the engine-wide check, outside the cold-start phase, that injectors on a direct-injection petrol engine really open when commanded. The module digitises the voltage across each injector and looks for the small kink the moving armature leaves; if commanded pulses repeatedly show no opening, it assumes fuel was not delivered.
s: Check engine light after two drives with the fault
Misfire or rough running if fuel is really missing
Often other codes from the same harness or injector fault
c: Engine harness chafed against underhood parts (GM 2.7 l L3B)
Engine software detecting falsely, fixed by reprogramming
Injector armature sticking or injector worn
High resistance in an injector circuit or connector

P2B97.d: P2B97 concerns the electrically driven exhaust back-pressure flap of GM's 3.0-litre Duramax diesel. After key-off the module moves the flap to its fully closed and fully open stops and stores what the SENT position sensor reports there.
s: Check engine light after one drive
Slower warm-up or reduced exhaust heating for aftertreatment
Possibly reduced engine power
c: Flap travel blocked by welding slag, soot or corrosion
Position sensor in the actuator drifted
Actuator gear or motor worn so the stops are not reached
Weak battery during the key-off learn

P2B98.d: P2B98 says the motor of exhaust pressure control valve A is not getting enough supply voltage. On GM's 3.0-litre Duramax, whose 2025 table 25OBDG04B documents the code, the H-bridge that drives the exhaust flap reports undervoltage below 6 V; 240 failed out of 300 samples taken every 12.5 ms set it, outside cranking and with the powertrain relay delivering more than 11 V.
s: Check engine light after one drive
Exhaust flap without function, slower warm-up
Further codes for the same fuse or harness
c: Blown fuse or interrupted feed to the valve actuator
Corroded connector or poor ground at the actuator
Weak battery or charging fault causing voltage dips

P2B99.d: P2B99 reports that the output stage driving exhaust pressure control valve A is running too hot or carrying too much current. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B for the 3.0-litre Duramax, the H-bridge driver temperature has to exceed 170 °C in 240 of 300 samples at 12.5 ms intervals, outside cranking and with more than 11 V on the powertrain relay; Type A, one trip.
s: Check engine light after one drive
Exhaust flap no longer controlled
Possibly reduced power or longer warm-up
c: Valve motor with internal fault such as shorted windings
Flap binding from soot or corrosion so the motor stalls
Defective driver stage in the control module

P2B9A.d: P2B9A covers a DEF quality sensor whose signal drops out now and then or jumps between values, rather than sitting permanently too low or too high. The sensor in the tank module usually gauges urea concentration by timing an ultrasonic echo and passes the result on digitally.
s: Check engine light on
DEF warning message, possibly a countdown to reduced speed or no restart
Fault comes and goes, often after refilling or on rough roads
c: Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at the DEF tank module
Air bubbles or sloshing DEF disturbing the ultrasonic echo
Urea crystals or deposits on the sensor face

P2B9B.d: P2B9B is a status code of the particulate matter sensor behind the diesel particulate filter: the sensor needs to burn its electrodes clean before the next measurement, but operating conditions do not allow it. Heating the ceramic to around 780 °C is only safe once the exhaust is dry.
s: Usually no change in driving
Particulate filter monitor shown as not complete
Code disappears after a longer drive at steady speed
c: Short trips and long idling keeping exhaust below the dew point
Faulty exhaust temperature signal misjudging dew point conditions
Low supply voltage to the sensor control unit preventing heating
Engine software setting the enable conditions too narrowly

P2B9C.d: P2B9C signals that coolant pump A is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn, or stops. Ford uses the code in its 2024 gasoline OBD summary as fault type 71 (actuator stuck) under P2600, where pump A is the auxiliary pump in the high-temperature loop for cabin heating; the check runs continuously above 11 V battery voltage over 5 seconds.
s: Little or no cabin heat
Check engine light
Pump silent when it should run
c: Seized bearing or rotor in the auxiliary pump
Sludge, sealant residue or debris jamming the impeller
Coolant frozen in the pump due to weak antifreeze
Burnt motor winding or failed drive electronics

P2B9D.d: P2B9D means the power feed of coolant pump A is outside its usable range, as opposed to the command line covered by P2600 to P2603. Ford names it in the 2024 gasoline OBD summary as fault type 1C (feed voltage outside its window) of the cabin-heating auxiliary pump, monitored all the time from 11 V battery voltage with a 5-second window.
s: Cabin heat weak or missing
Check engine light
Fault comes and goes with battery condition or electrical load
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump supply
Corroded connector or poor ground at the pump
Weak battery or charging system voltage too low

P2B9E.d: P2B9E is raised by the electronics built into coolant pump A when their temperature gets too high; the pump then derates or shuts down to protect itself. Ford's 2024 OBD summary for gasoline engines lists it as fault type 98 (system over temperature) of the cabin-heating auxiliary pump, monitored continuously once the battery supplies 11 V or more.
s: Cabin heat drops off after some time of driving
Check engine light
Pump stops and restarts after cooling down
c: Low coolant or air at the pump, so the electronics lose cooling
Stiff bearing or impeller raising motor load
Heat from nearby exhaust parts or damaged heat shield
Ageing power stage in the pump electronics

P2B9F.d: P2B9F means coolant pump B turns slower than requested. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary places it as underspeed type B2 in the block of base code P261A, where pump B is the auxiliary pump of the high-temperature loop for component cooling no.
s: Check engine light
Temperature warning for the cooled component under load
Possible power reduction to protect hot parts
c: Worn bearing or dragging impeller in pump B
Debris or sludge slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
Weak motor or drive electronics in the pump

P2BA0.d: P2BA0 reports that coolant pump C does not reach its speed. GM names the code Low Temperature Coolant Loop Pump Underspeed in its diesel ECM tables and treats it as a low out-of-range speed reading: in 2020 (20OBDG04) the printed limit is below -100 rpm in 5 of 8 one-second samples, in 2025 (25OBDG04A) below -50 rpm in 4 of 5; enable conditions are an active pump, 11 V or more at the relay and no cranking.
s: Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Parts on the low-temperature loop cooled less, reduced power possible
Further electrical codes when the harness is damaged
c: Engine harness chafed against brackets, shorting pump circuits
Worn or partly seized low-temperature loop pump
Air or low coolant in the low-temperature loop
Low supply voltage at the pump relay

P2BA1.d: P2BA1 is set when coolant pump D, a further electric pump in the manufacturer's thermal management, turns slower than its command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so which circuit pump D serves and which limits apply is unknown.
s: Check engine light or cooling warning, depending on the vehicle
Rising temperature of the part cooled by pump D
c: Worn bearing or dragging impeller in pump D
Debris or deposits slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or high resistance in power or ground
Weak motor or drive electronics in the pump

P2BA2.d: P2BA2 belongs to the electric main water pump. GM uses it in a way the title does not suggest: on the 2.7-litre L3B (table 19OBDG03D) and in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B the test runs while the pump should be switched off – pump disabled or a request of 0–4 rpm for at least 3 s – and fails if the pump still reports 10 rpm or more for 8 of 10 seconds with over 11 V on board.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Engine takes longer to reach operating temperature
Pump audible after the engine is switched off
c: Pump electronics ignoring the off command
Implausible speed feedback from the pump
Impeller turned by coolant flow from another pump
Command or enable line fault keeping the pump on

P2BA3.d: P2BA3 concerns the belt-driven starter-generator of mild-hybrid and stop-start engines: the controller has concluded that the machine does not turn the crankshaft or take torque from it as it should, although its electrics seem healthy. The exact detection rule is not published.
s: Squealing, chirping or grinding from the belt drive, often at start
Engine fails to restart after an automatic stop
Battery runs flat because the machine no longer charges
Electrical system warning or MIL on the instrument panel
c: Weak or defective belt tensioner or tensioner damper letting the belt slip
Worn, misaligned or thrown poly-V belt
Mechanical damage in the starter-generator (bearing, pulley)

P2BA4.d: Many diesel SCR systems rely on the oxidation catalyst ahead of them to turn part of the NO into NO2, because a mix near half NO2 lets the SCR reaction run fast at low temperature. P2BA4 reports that this catalyst no longer delivers the needed gas mix.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
SCR efficiency codes such as P20EE set as well
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: Oxidation catalyst thermally aged or poisoned (sulphur, oil ash), little NO2 produced
Catalyst inlet face coated with soot or unburnt fuel after injector or EGR problems
Faulty NOx or exhaust temperature sensor distorting the evaluation
Exhaust leak upstream of the catalyst diluting the measured gas

P2BA5.d: Some diesel particulate filters carry a precious-metal coating that, besides helping burn soot, oxidises NO to NO2 for the SCR catalyst further down. P2BA5 says this coated filter fails to supply enough NO2.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
More frequent active regenerations
SCR efficiency codes may follow
c: Filter coating thermally aged, e.g. after very hot or uncontrolled regenerations
Ash or oil additives covering the catalytic layer
Weak upstream oxidation catalyst in a combined evaluation
Exhaust temperature or NOx sensor reading wrongly

P2BA6.d: P2BA6 opens the group of NOx exceedance codes that grew out of the European rules on reagent-based NOx control. Each code names why tailpipe NOx has climbed above the diagnostic limit; here the blame lies with the SCR catalyst itself, while dosing, reagent and EGR still look plausible.
s: MIL and emission system warning in the cluster
Countdown to speed limit or no restart after some distance
Higher DEF consumption without better NOx reduction
c: SCR catalyst aged, overheated or chemically poisoned
Urea crystal deposits on mixer or catalyst face
Too little NO2 from upstream oxidation catalyst

P2BA7.d: P2BA7 records that NOx control has been lost because the DEF or AdBlue tank has run dry, so no reagent can be dosed. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI requires a level warning no later than 2,400 km ahead of an empty tank and an inducement that keeps the vehicle from operating with an empty tank, typically by blocking the next engine start after a countdown.
s: DEF empty message with restart countdown
Engine will not restart once countdown expires
MIL or emission warning on
c: DEF tank simply not refilled despite level warnings
Level sensor reading empty although fluid is present (fault, ice, deposits)
Leaking DEF tank or line emptying the system
Only a small amount refilled, below the quantity the system needs to recognise a refill

P2BA8.d: With P2BA8 the controller states that NOx went up because reagent dosing stopped although the engine needed it. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI, point 5.5, treats such an interruption as a case for the driver warning, unless the system paused dosing on purpose in conditions the maker declared to the authority; if dosing is not restored within 50 km, inducement starts.
s: DEF dosing malfunction message with distance countdown
MIL on, further SCR component codes stored
Reduced power or no restart if not repaired
c: DEF injector clogged or stuck by crystals
Pump failure or pressure not built up
Frozen fluid because tank or line heater fails
Wiring or SCR control unit fault stopping dosing

P2BA9.d: P2BA9 blames high NOx on reagent that falls short of the specified quality, e.g. diluted or contaminated DEF.
s: Incorrect DEF quality message with restart countdown
MIL on, often with P2BAE and P2BAF
Speed or power limit if the countdown runs out
c: DEF diluted with water, aged or replaced by the wrong fluid
Contaminated tank or lines (also from production, FCA 25-003-15)
Air leak after the MAF sensor or at EGR cooler joints misleading the NOx model (JLR)
Outdated engine software or faulty NOx sensor

P2BAA.d: P2BAA means less reagent is actually reaching the exhaust than the dosing strategy asks for, so NOx stays too high. EU Annex XVI sets the frame: actual and demanded consumption are compared, and a gap above 50 % over 30 minutes triggers the warning.
s: Service emission or exhaust fluid system message
MIL on after one trip
DEF level falls more slowly than usual
c: Partially blocked DEF injector delivering too little
Weak DEF pump or clogged pump filter
Calibration error setting the code without a fault (GM 25-NA-042)
Leak in the pressure line returning fluid before the injector

P2BAB.d: P2BAB attributes excess NOx to exhaust gas recirculation that delivers the wrong amount of gas, so combustion temperature and raw NOx rise. It belongs to the European NOx control rules: Regulation (EU) No 582/2011, Annex XIII, handles tampering-related monitoring through UN Regulation 49 and keeps an EGR valve counter, so an impeded valve leads to warning and inducement.
s: MIL on, EGR flow codes stored
Rough running or sooting with too much EGR
Power reduction possible if not repaired
c: EGR valve sooted up or sticking
EGR cooler or pipe partly blocked
Faulty EGR position sensor or air mass meter distorting flow estimate
Leak in the intake or EGR path

P2BAC.d: P2BAC is reserved for the case where exhaust gas recirculation is not just off target but shut down altogether, whether by an unplugged valve, a blocked path, an unauthorised software change or a defect that leaves the valve closed. The European rules treat this as a typical tampering scenario: Regulation (EU) No 582/2011, Annex XIII, carries an EGR valve counter that ends first in a warning and then in inducement.
s: MIL and NOx warning, later inducement
Harder, louder combustion
EGR circuit or position codes stored as well
c: EGR valve unplugged, blanked off or disabled
EGR valve stuck closed or actuator failed
Modified engine software with EGR switched off
Open or short in the EGR valve circuit

P2BAD.d: P2BAD is the catch-all of the series: NOx after the SCR is measured too high, yet none of the specific causes from P2BA6 to P2BAC can be pinned down. GM uses it on the 2014 Duramax 6.6 L LML as Exhaust NOx Concentration High - Unknown Reason: the measured SCR efficiency, minus an offset-corrected model value, is filtered over time and fails once the difference drops below zero, with both NOx sensors active for over 6
s: Exhaust fluid quality poor or emission warning
MIL on after the first failed run
Speed limit countdown if the condition persists
c: Poor DEF quality or partly blocked dosing without a specific code
Upstream or downstream NOx sensor drifting
Engine control software needing an update (Nissan Titan XD)

P2BAE.d: P2BAE is tied to the system that watches NOx control itself, typically the NOx sensors and the logic that compares measured emissions with the permitted level. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI allows exhaust NOx sensors to replace separate quality and consumption checks, with warning and inducement once the NOx OBD limit is passed; the heavy-duty rules keep counters for monitoring system faults.
s: MIL with DEF dosing malfunction message
No-restart countdown in the cluster
Stored together with P2BAF and a root cause code
c: Underlying SCR fault such as poor DEF quality or dosing pressure deviation
NOx sensor damaged, badly mounted or contaminated
Air trapped in the DEF system

P2BAF.d: P2BAF does not name a faulty part; it states that the driver inducement of the NOx control system has been activated. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI requires such an inducement once reagent is lacking, of wrong quality, under-consumed or not dosed, typically counting down to a blocked engine restart; the reason and the distance driven with it go into non-erasable records kept for 30,000 km or 800 days.
s: Countdown message until no restart
MIL and DEF system warning on
Speed or power limited, engine may not restart
c: Active SCR fault (DEF quality, dosing, level) that started the inducement
Control module software fault, e.g. BCM on Jeep Compass (FCA 08-103-19)
Root cause fixed but the clearing monitor has not yet run

P2BB0.d: On engines that burn compressed natural gas, LPG or another fuel besides petrol or diesel, the controller can estimate how much gas it has injected and compare that with how fast the tank actually empties, judged by tank pressure or level. P2BB0 means the tank drains noticeably more slowly than the injection quantity implies.
s: MIL on, sometimes together with lean mixture codes
Gas range or gauge reading implausible
Engine switches to petrol more often than usual
c: Alternative fuel tank pressure or temperature sensor reading wrong
Gas injectors or filter restricted, less gas delivered than commanded
Pressure regulator supplying too little pressure
Fuel mode or control software not matching actual operation

P2BB1.d: P2BB1 is set when the alternative fuel store, typically a CNG cylinder, loses more gas than the injected quantity can account for. The main suspicion is a leak between tank and injectors, which is why this check doubles as a safety monitor.
s: Gas range much shorter than usual
Gas smell around the vehicle
MIL on, gas mode may be locked out
c: Gas leak at fittings, lines, regulator or tank valve
Gas injector leaking or sticking open
Tank pressure or temperature sensor exaggerating the pressure drop

P2BB2.d: P2BB2 reports that the tank for the second fuel, mostly CNG or LPG, has been drawn down to its usable minimum. It is a status message rather than a component fault: a bi-fuel vehicle simply goes back to petrol.
s: Engine runs on petrol only, gas mode cannot be selected
Gas gauge shows empty or low-level warning
c: Gas tank actually used up to its reserve
Tank pressure or level sensor reading too low
Tank shutoff valve closed or not opening

P2BB3.d: Where a separate driver module powers the fuel pump, the ECM sends a duty-cycle command and the module reports what it actually applies. P2BB3 means these two values disagree beyond a tolerance, so the pump is not running at the requested speed although no open or short has been found.
s: MIL on
Hesitation or power loss under load
Long cranking or stalling
c: Fuel pump driver or tank zone module not delivering the commanded output
High resistance in the pump supply or ground connection
Worn or binding fuel pump drawing abnormal current
Disturbed data link between ECM and pump module

P2BB4.d: This code covers jumps in the signal of the fourth coolant temperature sensor that coolant cannot physically make. GM explains the method in the 2019 edition of its engine tables for the L3B and related engines (19OBDG03D): from each reading and the sensor's time constant the software predicts an upper and a lower bound for the next sample, and a step beyond either counts as erratic; 5 s of failures inside a 6 s wind
s: MIL on after two drives
Jumping temperature value in live data
Cooling fans or thermal management reacting erratically
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor 4 connector
Engine harness chafed, wire making intermittent contact
Internal intermittent break in the sensor element

P2BB5.d: P2BB5 is the erratic-signal code for coolant sensor 5. Unlike the hard circuit faults P2B2D and P2B2E, the reading here stays within the valid range but changes faster than the sensor's thermal inertia allows, which betrays a contact that briefly opens or shorts.
s: MIL on after the second trip
Sensor 5 value spikes in live data
Often stored together with other harness-related codes
c: Chafed engine harness with intermittent contact in the sensor 5 wires
Loose, spread or corroded connector terminal

P2BB6.d: P2BB6 is the general circuit code for a sixth coolant temperature sensor, intended for control units that only know that the circuit is faulty and do not distinguish a grounded from an open or shorted-high line. Six or more coolant sensors appear on engines with split cooling, rotary coolant valves or separate branches for head, block, radiator and heater; which physical sensor gets number 6 is the manufacturer's dec
s: MIL on
Sensor 6 shows a fixed substitute or implausible value
Fans may run continuously as a precaution
c: Sensor 6 connector unplugged, damaged or corroded
Open or shorted wire between sensor 6 and the ECM

P2BB7.d: With P2BB7 the sixth coolant sensor delivers an electrically valid value that nevertheless makes no sense. Plausibility tests of this kind compare the sensor with the other engine temperatures after a long cold soak, expect a clear rise once the engine warms up, and flag a value that never moves.
s: MIL on, usually only after a cold start and warm-up
Sensor 6 value lags or stays flat compared with the other coolant sensors
c: Sensor 6 element drifted out of its characteristic curve
No coolant flow at sensor 6 due to failed pump, valve or air pocket
Contact resistance at connector or terminals

P2BB8.d: Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low signal from sensor 6 means a very small resistance that the ECM would have to read as extreme heat; in practice a signal wire touching ground or a shorted element. GM sets P2BB8 when the sixth coolant channel drops below 47.5 Ω in its 2019 L3B/common tables (19OBDG03D) or 55 Ω in the 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B), both roughly equal to 150 °C, if that persists for 5 of any
s: MIL on after two trips
Sensor 6 shows an implausibly high temperature
Radiator fans running at high speed
c: Sensor 6 signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed harness
Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging the pins

P2BB9.d: A high signal from coolant sensor 6 corresponds to a resistance so large that only an interrupted circuit, a disconnected plug or a wire shorted to a voltage source explains it; read as temperature it would be colder than −60 °C. GM's tables check for this once the engine has run more than 10 s or intake air is warmer than −20 °C.
s: MIL on after the second trip
Sensor 6 shows about −40 °C or lower
Fans may run continuously
c: Sensor 6 connector unplugged or not latched
Broken signal or ground wire, or signal shorted to voltage

P2BBA.d: P2BBA catches short dropouts or spikes in the sixth coolant sensor signal that never last long enough to count as a steady low or high fault. GM includes it in its 2019 L3B/common ECM tables (19OBDG03D) and in the 2025 edition (25OBDG03B): based on the last reading and the sensor time constant, the software allows only a limited change per sample, and if the signal leaps past that window for 5 s within 6 s the code i
s: MIL on after two trips, may go out again
Sensor 6 value jumps in live data
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time
c: Chafed engine harness with intermittent contact
Loose or corroded terminal at sensor 6 or the ECM
Sensor element with intermittent internal break

P2BBB.d: P2BBB is the general fault of the position feedback from bypass valve A, the electrically driven valve that lets boosted air flow back from the compressor outlet to its inlet when the throttle closes or boost has to be trimmed. It is not the wastegate on the exhaust side.
s: Check engine light
Reduced boost and noticeably less power
Whoosh or flutter noise when lifting off the throttle
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the bypass valve position sensor
Chafed or broken signal, reference or ground wire in the harness near the compressor
Internal fault of the position sensor in the valve actuator
Faulty sensor input or 5 V reference inside the engine control module

P2BBC.d: P2BBC sets when the position signal of the bypass valve A sensor sits too low – usually an open signal wire, a short to ground or a lost 5 V supply to the sensor. GM uses the code on the 2019 Corvette ZR1 with the supercharged LT5, whose electronic compressor recirculation valve (eCRV) reports its position as a share of the reference voltage: a raw value under 10 % in 10 of 14 samples taken every 100 ms counts as a f
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Limited boost and weaker acceleration
Possibly further 5 V reference codes if the supply is shorted
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against the engine
Open 5 V reference wire or reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply
Pushed-out or corroded terminal in the valve connector
Defective position sensor in the valve actuator

P2BBD.d: P2BBD is the high-side counterpart: the position signal from bypass valve A rises toward the full reference voltage. That points to a short to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage, a broken sensor ground – the signal then floats upward – or a defective sensor.
s: Check engine light on immediately
Reduced power because boost is limited
Unusual noise when lifting off the throttle
c: Open sensor ground wire or corroded ground terminal
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Defective position sensor in the valve actuator
Moisture in the valve connector creating a leakage path

P2BBE.d: P2BBE is not a wiring fault but a failed end-stop learn. GM's 2019 tables for the LT5 Corvette ZR1 describe how the electronic recirculation valve is taught after each engine shutdown: the module first drives it to the closed stop and stores the sensor value, then repeats this for the open stop.
s: Check engine light after the engine has been switched off and restarted
Boost limited or erratic on lift-off
c: Oil or carbon deposits keeping the valve from reaching its stops
Bent flap or shaft, or worn actuator gear
Position sensor shifted or drifted after a repair or with age
Non-matching replacement valve with a different travel range

P2BBF.d: P2BBF concerns the power side of bypass valve A rather than its position feedback. Electric recirculation valves are moved by a small DC motor fed through an H-bridge in the engine module, and the bridge chip itself flags when its supply drops too far.
s: Check engine light on immediately
Valve no longer moves, boost limited or surging on lift-off
Often accompanied by other low-voltage codes
c: High resistance in the engine module feed, fuse or ground connection
Weak battery or charging fault causing voltage dips
Corroded pins at the engine module or valve connector
Internal fault of the H-bridge driver in the engine module

P2BC0.d: P2BC0 sets when the output stage that drives bypass valve A reports too much current or overheating. GM applies it to the electric recirculation valve of the LT5-powered 2019 Corvette ZR1: when the H-bridge raises its flag in 80 out of 100 checks spaced 12.5 ms apart, with relay voltage of 11 V or more and no cranking, a Type A fault with immediate MIL results.
s: Check engine light on immediately
Reduced boost and less power
Compressor surge noise when lifting off
c: Sticking or jammed valve making the motor draw high current
Shorted winding in the valve actuator motor
Motor leads shorted to each other or to ground in the harness
Overheated or damaged H-bridge driver in the engine module

P2BC1.d: P2BC1 means the electric pump that circulates coolant through the charge air cooler loop is powered, but its rotor will not turn or stops under load; the pump electronics see high current at little or no speed and report this to the engine module. Audi documents the code as P2BC100 in bulletin 2080825 for 2025–2026 A5/S5 and Q5 models with engine codes DXBA and DXCA: after the car stood unused longer than two months,
s: Check engine light, often with a reduced-power message
Hot charge air and less power under load
No running noise from the pump during an actuator test
c: Rotor stuck after a long standstill (Audi bulletin 2080825)
Debris, deposits or a worn bearing blocking the impeller
Engine module software needing an update (FCA bulletins for Giulia/Stelvio)
Ice in the loop due to insufficient antifreeze

P2BC2.d: P2BC2 points to the power feed of charge air cooler pump A: the pump or its controller sees a supply that is missing or outside its working window. Typical causes are a blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, a broken or corroded feed or ground wire, or a water-damaged plug; a weak battery can contribute.
s: Check engine light or engine warning message
Pump does not run, charge air temperature rises
Reduced power in hot conditions or under load
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump feed
Broken or corroded supply or ground wire
Water ingress or corrosion in the pump connector

P2BC3.d: The control electronics of an electric coolant pump sit inside the pump body and are cooled by the liquid flowing through it. P2BC3 means the electronics of charge air cooler pump A report a temperature above their limit.
s: Check engine light or engine warning message
Pump runs slower or switches off, especially in hot weather
Hot charge air and reduced power
c: Low coolant level or air trapped in the low-temperature loop
Partly blocked impeller or worn bearing raising motor current
Fault in the pump's integrated electronics
Missing heat shield or pump placed close to hot engine parts

P2BC4.d: P2BC4 is the catch-all electrical code for positive contactor B of the charging system, the second charging switch on the plus side next to contactor A (P0D07). Which charging path B serves is up to the maker: Mercedes-Benz files its B codes under the DC charge connection unit of its plug-in hybrids, EQB and eSprinter, Mazda under the on-board charger branch of its two large plug-in SUVs, and Audi calls it charging c
s: DC fast charging or on-board charger charging (depending on design) refused
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
Driving usually still possible
c: Coil of positive contactor B open or shorted
Wiring or connector fault in the contactor B branch
Fault or software issue in the controlling module

P2BC5.d: P2BC5 reports that positive charging contactor B still conducts after the open command, normally because its contacts have fused. Mercedes-Benz stores it, often with P2BCC, in the DC charge connection unit (N116/5, on the eSprinter N24/6) of GLE, E- and S-Class plug-in hybrids, the EQB and the eSprinter; after a DC session the vehicle refuses to start.
s: Vehicle will not start after DC charging (Mercedes)
High-voltage or hybrid system warning in the cluster
Further charging blocked
c: Contacts of positive contactor B welded, e.g. after current peaks at the end of charging
Software of the charging module judges the contactor state wrongly (Mercedes update)
Ripple, overcurrent or overvoltage from the charging station
Coil driver does not switch off

P2BC6.d: P2BC6 means positive charging contactor B does not close when commanded, so the plus side of that charging branch stays dead and the session aborts or never starts. The only maker documenting it publicly is Mazda: on the 2024–2026 CX-90 and 2025–2026 CX-70 plug-in hybrids it reads OBC contactor (+) stuck off, listed with the welded cases P2BC5 and P2BCC.
s: Charging session stops or does not start
Hybrid system malfunction message (Mazda)
Driving usually unaffected
c: Contactor B damaged inside and no longer closing (Mazda junction box)
Coil supply or drive line interrupted
Charging control software misjudging the closing check

P2BC7.d: P2BC7 concerns the coil drive line of positive charging contactor B, not its main contacts: the module compares its command with the voltage and current it measures on that line and sets the code when the line is broken or the driver that does not follow. No manufacturer documents P2BC7 publicly.
s: Charging via the contactor B path not possible
Charging fault indication
c: Control wire or connector to contactor B interrupted
Coil of positive contactor B open
Driver stage in the control module defective

P2BC8.d: P2BC8 flags a control circuit of positive charging contactor B that is connected but behaves implausibly: the coil draws a current that does not fit the command, the line voltage lies in an unexpected band, or pulling in takes too long. No manufacturer documents P2BC8 publicly.
s: Charging works only now and then
Charging aborts with a fault message
c: Contact resistance at connectors of the control line
Coil resistance of contactor B outside specification
Driver stage in the module degraded

P2BC9.d: P2BC9 is the low-signal fault on the coil feed of plus-side charging contactor B: the module measures less voltage on that wire than its command calls for, most often because the wire touches ground or the output stage is being dragged down. With a high-side feed the coil is then starved and the contactor never pulls in, or the output stage trips its own protection.
s: Charging session does not start
Charging fault message
c: Control wire of contactor B shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in a connector
Coil of contactor B internally shorted

P2BCA.d: P2BCA means the wire energising the coil of positive charging contactor B shows too much voltage, caused by contact with battery voltage or an output stage stuck in the on state; the contactor could then pull in uncommanded. Audi documents the code as charging contactor 2, short to positive, in the hybrid battery management module (address 008C) of the 2024 Q8 and SQ8 e-tron, including Sportback.
s: Drive system cannot be activated after charging (Audi)
Drive system and electrical system fault warnings
Charging blocked
c: Control wire of contactor B shorted to supply voltage
Driver stage does not switch off

P2BCB.d: P2BCB is the general electrical code for negative contactor B of the charging system, which closes the return path of the second charging branch to the traction battery. No manufacturer documents P2BCB publicly.
s: Charging in the affected mode refused
Charging fault message
Driving usually still possible
c: Coil of negative contactor B open or shorted
Wiring or connector fault on the return-side contactor
Fault in the module that drives contactor B

P2BCC.d: P2BCC says negative charging contactor B is still closed although the module ordered it open – in practice fused contacts on the return side. Mercedes-Benz lists it in the DC charge connection unit next to P2BC5 and P0E8929 (DC input current too high); the plug-in hybrid, EQB or eSprinter then cannot be started after DC charging.
s: Vehicle will not start after DC charging (Mercedes)
High-voltage system warning
Charging blocked
c: Contacts of negative contactor B welded at the end of charging
Current ripple or overvoltage from the DC station

P2BCD.d: P2BCD is set when negative charging contactor B fails to close, so the charging branch lacks its return path and no current can flow even with the plus side connected. No manufacturer documents P2BCD publicly; Mazda lists the welded minus case P2BCC and the non-closing plus case P2BC6 for the CX-90 PHEV, but not this one.
s: Charging stops or never starts
Charging fault message
c: Negative contactor B burnt or mechanically not closing
Coil supply too weak or interrupted
Charging control software misjudging the check

P2BCE.d: P2BCE watches the coil drive of negative charging contactor B for an open line or a driver whose real state differs from its command. No manufacturer documents P2BCE publicly.
s: Charging via the contactor B path not possible
Charging fault indication
c: Control wire or terminal of negative contactor B open
Coil of negative contactor B open
Driver stage in the module defective

P2BCF.d: P2BCF points to a control circuit on negative charging contactor B that is neither open nor shorted yet still implausible: coil current, line voltage or switching time fall outside the window that belongs to the commanded state. No manufacturer documents P2BCF publicly, and no published GM table has such a check for a charging contactor coil.
s: Charging drops out or will not begin
Charging fault message from time to time
c: Coil resistance of negative contactor B shifted
Corrosion or contact resistance in the control connector
Poor ground of the controlling module

P2BD0.d: With P2BD0 the coil drive line of minus-side charging contactor B is too low – usually insulation damage letting the wire touch the body, or an output stage stuck low. Starved of current, the coil leaves the return path of that charging branch open.
s: Charging session will not start
Charging fault message
c: Control wire of negative contactor B shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector of the control line
Coil of negative contactor B internally shorted

P2BD1.d: P2BD1 flags excess voltage on the coil feed of minus-side charging contactor B, for instance from contact with a 12 V wire or an output stage that will not turn off. The risk is a coil that stays energised and keeps the return pole connected while the module believes it is open, so the module normally blocks charging.
s: Charging blocked
High-voltage or charging fault warning
c: Control wire of negative contactor B shorted to supply voltage

P2BD2.d: P2BD2 reports that the first aftertreatment line, or the only one, is not gas-tight, so exhaust escapes between engine and tailpipe or false air enters. A leak upstream of the catalysts lets untreated NOx and soot out and also confuses sensors: Foton Cummins patented a check that compares the measured aftertreatment pressure with a model value from exhaust back pressure and flags a leak beyond a limit, noting that le
s: MIL on
Exhaust smell, soot marks or ticking at a joint
Follow-up SCR or particulate filter codes
c: Loose V-band clamp or failed gasket between aftertreatment modules
Cracked exhaust pipe, flex joint or catalyst housing
Leak at a sensor, DEF injector or pressure tap mounting
Pressure sensor hose cracked, making the system look leaky

P2BD3.d: P2BD3 is the twin of P2BD2 for a second aftertreatment line, found on engines with two parallel exhaust paths, each with its own catalysts and filter. Which physical line is B is up to the maker; in practice it is usually the path of the second cylinder bank.
s: MIL on
Exhaust noise or smell on one side
Uneven readings between the two lines
c: Loose clamp or leaking gasket in line B
Crack in pipe, flex joint or housing on side B
Leaking sensor or injector mounting on line B
Faulty pressure sensor or hose shared by both lines

P2BD4.d: Hybrid and electric drives cool the inverter, DC/DC converter and motor with one or more electric pumps; J2012 labels them A, B and C. P2BD4 means the controlling module has found an open circuit or an unclassified fault on the control line of pump C.
s: Hybrid or drive system warning, often with the check engine light
Reduced drive power when the electronics heat up
Pump C silent during an actuator test
c: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at pump C
Broken control or signal wire between module and pump
Faulty output or input stage in the controlling module

P2BD5.d: P2BD5 flags the command line of the third electric coolant pump in the inverter and motor electronics loop as sitting at too low a level. With a low-side or PWM driver this usually means the wire or the pump input is shorted to ground, so the pump either runs unchecked or not at all.
s: Warning for the hybrid or drive system, often with the check engine light
Pump C runs constantly or stays silent regardless of command
Reduced drive power once the electronics warm up
c: Pump C control wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion in the pump connector bridging the signal pin to ground
Shorted input stage inside pump C
Faulty output driver in the controlling module

P2BD6.d: P2BD6 is stored when the control circuit of motor electronics coolant pump C reads higher than the commanded state allows. A short to battery voltage, or a driver stage that reports overcurrent, are the usual triggers; the pump may then keep running or ignore commands.
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Pump C keeps running after the vehicle is switched off, or does not respond at all
Power limitation during long climbs or fast driving
c: Control wire of pump C shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Pump C drawing excessive current because of an internal electrical fault
Bent or corroded pins in the pump C connector touching each other
Failed output stage in the controlling module

P2BD7.d: P2BD7 means pump C in the motor electronics cooling loop is electrically reachable but does not deliver what the controller asks for: wrong speed, a fault report from the pump itself or too little cooling effect. No manufacturer documents P2BD7 publicly.
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Cooling fan running at high speed more often than usual
Reduced electric drive or charging power when the loop gets warm
c: Air trapped in the electronics loop after a repair or coolant loss
Low coolant level in the electronics loop reservoir
Worn, sticking or debris-blocked pump C
Outdated software in the hybrid controller that misjudges the pump

P2BD8.d: Some hybrid and electric drives measure the coolant in the inverter and motor electronics loop at more than one point; J2012 names these sensors A, B and C, and which spot each letter marks is left to the manufacturer. P2BD8 is the general circuit code for sensor B: the signal cannot be used, but none of the specific low, high or plausibility verdicts applies.
s: Hybrid or drive system warning, often with the check engine light
Electronics coolant pump and fan running more than usual
Possible reduction of electric drive power
c: Loose, unplugged or corroded connector at sensor B
Damaged signal or reference wire between sensor B and the module
Faulty input circuit in the controlling module

P2BD9.d: P2BD9 means coolant temperature sensor B in the motor electronics loop delivers a voltage inside its electrical window, yet the temperature it reports does not fit the rest of the vehicle. The circuit itself is intact; a drifting thermistor, a sensor sitting in an air pocket or a value that stays frozen are typical.
s: Check engine light, usually without a noticeable driving issue at first
Cooling fan or electronics pump running at unexpected times
Occasional power limitation on hot days
c: Sensor B thermistor drifted out of its characteristic
Air pocket or low coolant leaving sensor B partly dry
Added resistance from corroded terminals shifting the reading
Wrong value from a comparison sensor such as engine coolant or intake air temperature

P2BDA.d: P2BDA is set when the sensor B signal in the electronics coolant loop falls below its valid window. These sensors are normally NTC thermistors, so a low voltage translates into an impossibly hot reading; a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor is the classic cause.
s: Check engine light and hybrid system warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly high electronics coolant temperature
Power reduction even with a cold vehicle
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Moisture in the sensor connector creating a leakage path to ground
Faulty input stage in the evaluating module

P2BDB.d: P2BDB tells that the signal of coolant temperature sensor B sits above its valid voltage range. With a thermistor fed from a 5 V reference through a pull-up resistor, a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a sensor gone open lets the voltage rise to almost the reference, which the module would read as extreme cold.
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly low electronics coolant temperature
Electronics coolant pump running at a fixed high speed
c: Sensor B connector unplugged, not latched or with a backed-out pin
Broken signal or ground wire of sensor B
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source

P2BDC.d: P2BDC reports a general fault in the circuit of coolant temperature sensor C, a third measuring point that some drives use in the loop cooling the inverter, converter and motor. The code stands for a signal the module cannot use without assigning it to the low, high or plausibility codes P2BDE, P2BDF and P2BDD.
s: Warning lamp for the hybrid or drive system
Fan and electronics pump running at high output as a precaution
Possibly reduced electric power
c: Poor contact at the sensor C connector
Chafed or broken wiring between sensor C and the module
Fault on a 5 V reference or sensor ground shared with other sensors

P2BDD.d: P2BDD is the plausibility check of coolant temperature sensor C: electrically the signal looks fine, but the reported value cannot be right when set against other temperatures. No manufacturer documents P2BDD publicly.
s: Check engine light without an obvious drivability problem
Cooling fan behaviour that does not match the conditions
Power or charging limitation under heavy load
c: Sensor C reading drifted away from the true coolant temperature
Air or weak flow at the sensor C location, so it sees a local hot or cold spot
Corroded terminals adding resistance in the sensor C circuit
Faulty comparison temperature from another sensor in the system

P2BDE.d: P2BDE reports that the voltage from coolant temperature sensor C has dropped below its lower limit. Low describes the voltage: for the usual NTC sensor it corresponds to a reading far hotter than the coolant can be, and the cause is mostly a grounded signal wire, a crushed pigtail or a sensor that has shorted internally.
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Very high electronics coolant temperature shown in live data on a cold vehicle
Fan running at full speed shortly after start
c: Sensor C signal wire shorted to ground or to the sensor ground
Crushed or melted sensor pigtail near hot components
Faulty analog input in the evaluating module

P2BDF.d: P2BDF is stored when the signal of coolant temperature sensor C climbs to nearly the full reference voltage. For the module this looks like coolant colder than any climate allows; in practice a pin that has backed out of the connector, a corroded or broken signal wire, or a short to a voltage source is behind it.
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning
Live data shows the lowest possible temperature for sensor C
Pump and fan running in a fixed protective mode
c: Backed-out or loose pin in the sensor C connector
Corroded or broken signal wire of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or another supply

P2BE0.d: P2BE0 concerns the wiring of the level sensor in the coolant reservoir of the high-voltage battery loop: its signal is missing or the line is broken. Stellantis documents the code as P2BE0-00 on the 2021-22 Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid, where the cluster asks for hybrid system service; Tech Tip 9004552 tells dealers to photograph the level in the battery coolant bottle before swapping sensor or bottle, so the real level
s: Service hybrid system message on the cluster
MIL on
Plug-in charging disabled on some models
c: Battery coolant level actually low (leak or after service), bulletin asks to check first
Level sensor defective, e.g. internal solder joints (GM Volt)
Open signal wire or loose connector at the reservoir
Internal break in the sensor jumper harness

P2BE1.d: P2BE1 reports a battery coolant level signal that lies inside the electrical limits yet makes no sense, such as a value between the defined full and low states or one that flickers while the vehicle stands still. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning, often intermittent
MIL on
Coolant level looks correct at the reservoir
c: Level sensor with internal fault, e.g. cracked solder joints
Intermittent contact in connector or jumper harness
Coolant level near the switching point or air in the loop
Evaluation software in the battery or hybrid controller

P2BE2.d: P2BE2 is stored when the voltage from the battery coolant level sensor falls below the lowest value the sensor can legitimately produce. That points to the signal touching ground or a sensor whose output collapses, not to a low coolant level, which normally reads inside the valid range.
s: Hybrid system warning
MIL on
Charging possibly disabled
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground

P2BE3.d: P2BE3 means the level sensor signal of the battery coolant loop is above its valid range, typically from a short to the sensor supply or to 12 V, or from a lost sensor ground. No manufacturer documents P2BE3 publicly.
s: Hybrid system warning
MIL on
Charging possibly disabled
c: Signal wire shorted to sensor supply or 12 V
Open sensor ground or open signal with pull-up (read as high)

P2BE4.d: P2BE4 is the general circuit code for a third current measurement in the high-voltage battery, used where sensor A (P0ABF to P0AC3) and sensor B (P0B0E to P0B13) are already taken. What C measures depends on the design: a further Hall or shunt channel, or a sensor in a second current path; Continental patents a battery busbar with three independent current devices whose values are compared.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced electric power or range
MIL on
c: Wiring or connector fault between sensor and battery controller
Input stage or software of the battery controller

P2BE5.d: P2BE5 flags current sensor C as implausible although its signal is electrically valid, for instance an offset with no current flowing or a value at odds with the other readings. Stellantis lists it, worded as current sensor C circuit performance, in bulletins 08-047-20 and 08-130-21 for the 2017-18 Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrid with the 3.6 litre engine: the MIL comes on, and the remedy is new software for the bat
s: MIL on
Hybrid system warning
Inaccurate state of charge or reduced electric range
c: Battery controller software (Stellantis Pacifica PHEV, reflash per bulletin)
High resistance at connector or sensor ground

P2BE6.d: P2BE6 is set when the output of current sensor C drops below the lowest value it can deliver in normal service. Unlike its A and B siblings, the official title omits the word circuit, but the meaning is the same out-of-range low check.
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Reduced power, possibly no ready mode

P2BE7.d: With P2BE7 the signal of current sensor C sits above its usable range, which after conversion would be an impossibly large current. As with P2BE6, the official wording drops the word circuit.
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Battery power limited
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V supply or 12 V

P2BE8.d: P2BE8 reports an open in control circuit B of the battery precharge function, i.e. the coil drive of a second precharge contactor.
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Charging not possible
c: Open control wire or loose connector at contactor B
Coil of precharge contactor B open internally
Driver stage in the battery controller defective

P2BE9.d: P2BE9 says control circuit B of the precharge function is connected but behaves implausibly: the coil current, the feedback voltage or the effect of switching does not match the command. No manufacturer documents P2BE9 publicly.
s: Vehicle sometimes does not become ready
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
c: Coil resistance out of tolerance or sluggish armature
High-voltage load or resistor fault keeping the bus from rising during precharge
Corrosion or high resistance in the control circuit
Battery controller software or driver stage

P2BEA.d: P2BEA is stored when control circuit B of the precharge function carries less voltage than its state requires, mostly because the coil feed touches ground or the output is pulled down. With a high-side driver the coil then gets no current and the second precharge path stays open.
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
c: Coil feed chafed and shorted to ground
Coil of precharge contactor B shorted internally
Driver stage of the battery controller pulled low

P2BEB.d: P2BEB reports too much voltage on control circuit B of the precharge function while it should be off, usually a short to 12 V or a driver that does not switch off. The risk is a second precharge path closing on its own; the resistor can overheat if it stays in circuit.
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
High-voltage system blocked as a precaution
c: Driver stage stuck on in the battery controller
Damaged insulation between adjacent wires in the harness

P2BEC.d: Engines that combine port and direct injection keep separate fuel trim adaptations for each injection mode. Ford, which uses this code on its PFDI engines such as the 2.7 L EcoBoost and 5.0 L V8 of the F-150, assigns system A to the direct-injection mode.
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation under acceleration, when the engine relies on direct injection
Often no noticeable change in drivability
c: PCM software fault on affected Ford models, fixed by reprogramming
High-pressure pump or its volume regulator delivering too little rail pressure
Direct injectors on bank 1 restricted or coked
Bank 1 upstream oxygen sensor reading skewed

P2BED.d: P2BED is the rich counterpart of P2BEC: bank 1 has to remove fuel, but only while the engine is fed by direct injection, which Ford calls fuel system A on its port-plus-direct engines. The Ford monitor runs continuously in closed loop and reacts when long-term trim has pulled more than 25 percent and short-term trim keeps pulling beyond 1 percent for 2 seconds; purge must be off, so a saturated canister is not the re
s: Check engine light on
Long cranking or rough running right after a hot start
Fuel smell from the exhaust, higher consumption
Misfire codes on the same bank in some cases
c: Direct injector leaking or dribbling on bank 1
PCM software fault, Ford reprogramming bulletins
Rail pressure above target because of a faulty volume regulator or pressure sensor

P2BEE.d: Here the lean correction concerns bank 2, the cylinder row without cylinder 1, and again only the direct-injection operating mode (fuel system A in Ford terms). Ford applies the same monitor as on bank 1: closed loop, warm engine, purge off, long-term trim above plus 25 percent combined with short-term trim above plus 1 percent for 2 seconds.
s: Check engine light on
Slight hesitation under load
Often no other complaint
c: PCM software requiring a Ford update
Bank 2 upstream oxygen sensor reading skewed
Low rail pressure, usually with P2BEC on bank 1 too

P2BEF.d: P2BEF says that the engine module has had to take away a lot of fuel on bank 2 while direct injection alone was supplying the cylinders. Ford sets it on port-plus-direct engines when long-term trim on that bank drops past minus 25 percent while short-term trim keeps subtracting more than 1 percent; two seconds in closed loop are enough.
s: Check engine light on
Rough running after a hot restart
Increased fuel use
c: Known PCM software issue on 2019-2020 F-150 2.7 L
Direct injector on bank 2 sticking open or seeping
Rail pressure sensor reading too low, pressure actually too high

P2BF0.d: Fuel system B is, in Ford's monitor documents, the port fuel injection mode of engines that also have direct injectors. P2BF0 therefore means bank 1 runs lean only when the port injectors do the work.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven idle or surging at light load
Hesitation when pulling away
c: Low-pressure fuel pump or supply pressure too weak for the port injectors
Air leak at a port injector O-ring or intake manifold gasket

P2BF1.d: With P2BF1 the PCM has seen bank 1 too rich while fuel came through the port injectors, Ford's fuel system B. Ford flags it when the long-term value sits beyond minus 25 percent and the short-term value still takes away above 1 percent, for a 2 second window in closed loop.
s: Check engine light on
Fuel smell, black exhaust deposits
Rough idle when warm
c: Port injector on bank 1 leaking or dribbling

P2BF2.d: P2BF2 combines two restrictions: the lean correction is on bank 2, and it only occurs in the port injection mode that Ford designates fuel system B. The Ford threshold is identical to the other trim codes of this family, more than 25 percent added by long-term trim plus over 1 percent by short-term trim for 2 seconds.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven idle
Mild hesitation at part throttle
c: Air leak at the bank 2 intake gasket or injector O-ring
Weak low-pressure supply, usually with P2BF0 as well

P2BF3.d: The last of the eight mode-specific trim codes: bank 2 is too rich while the port injectors (Ford fuel system B) are active. Ford triggers it when long-term trim has gone below minus 25 percent and short-term trim continues to subtract over 1 percent for 2 seconds, with the engine warm and purge disabled.
s: Check engine light on
Fuel smell at idle
Higher consumption
c: Port injector on bank 2 not sealing
Bank 2 upstream oxygen sensor biased lean

P2BF4.d: Many electrically driven exhaust flaps report their actual angle back to the engine computer, either as an analog voltage or as a PWM duty cycle from a smart actuator. P2BF4 is the umbrella fault for that feedback path on valve A: the signal is missing, unusable or cannot be classed as clearly too low or too high.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust flap no longer switched, sound stays in one mode
c: Actuator connector loose, wet or corroded by road salt
Feedback or ground wire broken or heat-damaged near the exhaust
Position sensor inside the flap actuator failed

P2BF5.d: Here the position signal of exhaust valve A is electrically fine, yet its value does not fit: the reported angle disagrees with the command, the end stops are not where the learned values say, or the signal jumps. Ford lists P2BF5 in its active exhaust bulletins for the 2018-2023 Mustang (21-2011 for the 2020 GT500, later 23-2132 and 25-2146), together with the matching valve B code P2BFD and the drive codes.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode or drive mode not available message
Exhaust tone does not change between modes
c: Muffler or tailpipe not fully seated in its clamps, straining the actuator
Actuator bracket bent or not welded flush to the tailpipe
Pinched actuator harness giving an unstable signal
Flap shaft binding from corrosion or soot

P2BF6.d: P2BF6 means the position feedback of exhaust valve A sits below its valid range, as with a signal shorted to ground or a lost sensor supply. Mazda is the best documented user: its 2.5 litre Skyactiv-G with cylinder deactivation carries an exhaust shutter valve that Mazda patents describe as closing partly in two-cylinder mode to damp exhaust pulsation noise.
s: Master warning or check engine light on
Reduced engine power
c: PCM software misjudging the sensor (Mazda bulletin 01-004/20)
Position signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor supply open or connector not latched
Position sensor in the shutter valve failed

P2BF7.d: P2BF7 is set when the position feedback of exhaust valve A rises above its plausible maximum. Electrically that points to the signal line touching the sensor reference or battery voltage, or to a lost sensor ground, which lets the input float up to its pull-up level.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust flap held in its default position
Exhaust sound no longer changes as expected
c: Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Position sensor in the valve assembly failed

P2BF8.d: Valve B is the second exhaust flap; Ford's gasoline OBD summaries 2020-2024 put it on bank 2, while valve A (P26C5) serves bank 1. P2BF8 reports that the drive circuit for flap B is open or unusable.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode not available message
One tailpipe flap no longer moves
c: Broken or unplugged harness to the bank 2 flap actuator
Open circuit inside the flap actuator
Actuator not aligned after replacement or outdated PCM software (subtype 78)

P2BF9.d: With P2BF9 the control line of exhaust flap B is pulled toward ground. A bare spot rubbing on the body or exhaust, or a shorted actuator, is the classic cause, which is why the code tends to appear after exhaust work or with a sagging harness.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode cannot be changed
Bank 2 flap stuck, uneven sound left and right
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Harness pinched at the actuator bracket
Internal short in the flap B actuator

P2BFA.d: P2BFA reports too high a level on the control line of exhaust flap B. Either the wire has contact with a powered circuit, or the actuator electronics feed voltage back, so the driver cannot pull the line down when it should.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode warning in the cluster
Bank 2 flap in wrong position for the selected mode
c: Control wire shorted to a powered circuit
Flap B actuator electronics feeding voltage back
Damaged tailpipe actuator harness, Ford service part 14A411

P2BFB.d: P2BFB is the functional fault of flap B: wiring checks pass, but the flap does not reach or hold the commanded angle. Ford runs two tests on its bank 2 flap.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode not available message
No audible difference between exhaust modes
c: Flap B binding from corrosion, soot or ice
Exhaust or actuator bracket not seated correctly
Actuator not aligned or outdated PCM calibration

P2BFC.d: P2BFC covers a general fault in the feedback path that tells the engine computer where exhaust flap B is. It applies only to systems with a second position-monitored flap, such as one per tailpipe, so on single-flap vehicles it cannot occur.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode selection limited or unavailable
c: Flap B connector loose, wet or corroded
Feedback wire to flap B broken or heat-damaged
Position sensing in actuator B failed

P2BFD.d: P2BFD flags a position signal from exhaust flap B that is electrically valid but implausible, for instance an angle that lags the command, end points that drifted from the learned values, or a reading that wanders while the flap should rest. Ford is the public user.
s: Check engine light on
Drive mode or exhaust mode not available message
Exhaust tone stays the same in every mode
c: Muffler and tailpipe not fully engaged in the clamps
Actuator bracket not welded flush to the tailpipe

P2BFE.d: The position feedback of exhaust flap B reads below its lowest valid value. For an analog sensor that means a signal at or near 0 V, typically a short to ground or a missing 5 V supply; for a PWM feedback it means a duty cycle stuck near zero.
s: Check engine light on
Flap B no longer adjusted, exhaust sound unchanged
c: Flap B signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor reference supply open or shorted
Position sensor in actuator B failed

P2BFF.d: P2BFF is the upper limit fault for the position feedback of exhaust flap B. An analog signal pinned near supply voltage, or a PWM feedback stuck near 100 percent, usually comes from a lost sensor ground, a signal wire touching voltage, or water bridging the connector pins.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode warning, flap B held in default position
c: Open ground at the flap B position sensor
Water or salt bridging the actuator B connector pins
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
